blocks.text: **Phonemes are speech-sound categories, not letters.** A writing system represents language, but its symbols do not have to correspond one-to-one with those categories. A letter can contribute to different pronunciations, and a phoneme can be represented by different spellings.
**Keep spoken categories separate from written symbols.** Identifying a letter is not the same task as identifying a phoneme.
children: The question concerns the relation between sound and writing, rather than how many letters a word contains.

blocks.text: **Orthographic depth** describes how consistently spelling corresponds to pronunciation. English is relatively deep because many spellings do not transparently specify their sounds. COLONEL and PARADIGM make the problem concrete. Applying common letter–sound patterns can produce a plausible-looking pronunciation that is wrong for the actual word.
children: In shallower writing systems, such as Finnish and Korean, spelling–sound correspondences are more predictable. The comparison concerns the writing system, not the intelligence or ability of its readers.

blocks.text: **An unfamiliar spelling cannot always be decoded correctly from its letters alone.** Deep orthographies create more exceptions that readers must learn through experience.
children: The English examples contrast ordinary expectations from the letters with the word's learned pronunciation. A deep script is less predictable, not completely random.

blocks.text: **Finnish has a shallow orthography.** Letters correspond relatively unambiguously to phonemes, so learning a spelling–sound correspondence helps with many different words. Doubled letters represent a meaningful length distinction. A doubled consonant is geminated, and a doubled vowel is long.
children: This regularity helps Finnish children learn decoding quickly. Decoding means generating a pronunciation from a written form, whether or not its meaning is familiar.

blocks.text: **Consistent correspondences make decoding easier to generalize.** Finnish readers can apply what they learn about letters to unfamiliar written forms.
children: The linked Finnish lesson is a source demonstration. Its sound is not embedded in the PDF, so the written claims establish the correspondence and length distinctions without supplying a recovered recording.

blocks.text: **Pseudoword reading tests decoding.** Because a pseudoword is not a familiar stored word, the child must generalize from learned spelling–sound patterns. The comparison involves Grade 1 children learning different alphabetic writing systems. Children learning many other languages produce plausible pseudoword pronunciations more successfully than English learners.
children: English's less predictable correspondences help explain why decoding develops more slowly. This task does not measure the child's entire language ability.

blocks.text: **A made-up word separates decoding from remembering a familiar word.** The lower English performance is consistent with greater orthographic depth.
children: Compare accuracy across languages for the same type of task. The important outcome is the relative difficulty of English pseudoword decoding, not a claim that English children cannot decode.

blocks.text: **Korean writing represents sound structure systematically.** Related phonemes can have related written shapes, so the visual forms themselves reflect aspects of phonological organization. The letters are arranged into syllable blocks with initial, medial and sometimes final positions. Those positions are not three unrelated pictures of whole words.
children: The velar consonant forms share the basic angular ㄱ shape. Additional strokes or doubling distinguish related consonants.

blocks.text: **The organization of Hangul supports more than consistent pronunciation.** Similar sound categories can also be visibly related in their written symbols.
children: The diagrams label initial, medial and final positions. The g, kk and k examples share a shape family, illustrating how a place-of-articulation relation can be reflected in the script.

blocks.text: **GLORP, SPLING, JONK, FEESH and QUISP can be pronounced without being familiar words.** Their forms follow enough English spelling patterns for a reader to construct a plausible pronunciation. Success cannot depend on retrieving a stored pronunciation for each particular item. The reader is using knowledge that generalizes across words.
children: The demonstration establishes generalization. By itself, it does not decide whether that knowledge consists of categorical rules or learned statistical patterns.

blocks.text: **Reading a novel letter sequence reveals knowledge beyond memorized words.** Familiar spelling patterns support pronunciation of new combinations.
children: The items are instructional stimuli. Their role is to test decoding, not vocabulary knowledge or knowledge of a definition.

blocks.text: **Pseudoword decoding is fast and largely automatic.** In the Lupker, Brown and Colombo example, naming pseudowords is only about 5–12% slower than naming low-frequency real words. Participants read the items aloud, and naming time measures how quickly a pronunciation becomes available. The small difference shows that unfamiliarity does not make pronunciation an entirely slow, deliberate process.
children: Both rules and statistical generalization might produce efficient decoding. The speed result constrains a theory without selecting one architecture on its own.

blocks.text: **Fast nonword naming is evidence that decoding is a normal part of skilled reading.** It does not by itself prove that a separate rule system performs the task.
children: Compare pseudowords with low-frequency words rather than treating every real word as an equally familiar baseline. A percentage slowdown describes relative naming time, not an error rate.

blocks.text: **An unfamiliar spelling can support more than one plausible pronunciation.** VONTH, PHANGE, STREAD and SOUGH contain patterns whose pronunciations are not all uniquely determined in English. A response reflects the spelling–sound patterns available from previously learned words. Different familiar patterns can favor different responses to the same novel form.
**Generalization can be graded rather than all-or-none.** Ambiguous pseudowords reveal competing pronunciation possibilities.
children: These items probe how readers resolve uncertainty in spelling-to-sound mappings. There is no requirement that every unfamiliar form have one universally agreed pronunciation.

blocks.text: **STREAD can plausibly be pronounced with either /ɛ/ or /i/.** The same written sequence can resemble more than one learned spelling–sound pattern. Testing novel items reveals what a reader has generalized, because the particular word cannot simply have been memorized.
children: The challenge for a categorical rule account is to explain why multiple outputs seem acceptable. A statistical account can represent differing support for alternative pronunciations.

blocks.text: **Accepting both /strɛd/ and /strid/ is information about the knowledge being generalized.** A model must explain the alternatives, not merely choose one output and ignore the other.
children: The contrast changes the vowel while keeping the rest of STREAD constant. This isolates ambiguity in the spelling–sound relation.

blocks.text: **The regularity effect is the difficulty of reading words whose pronunciation conflicts with common spelling–sound patterns.** PINT, ACHE and CHOIR are examples of words for which straightforward decoding can mislead. A strict regular–irregular division is less clear when a spelling neighborhood contains several pronunciations. ROLL, POLL and TOLL support one pattern, while DOLL differs.
children: COOK, TOOK and BOOK likewise contrast with SPOOK. These neighborhoods motivate asking how much support a pronunciation has from similar words.

blocks.text: **A word's difficulty depends partly on how its spelling neighbors are pronounced.** The issue is not simply whether the reader knows the letters.
children: A neighborhood is a set of words sharing relevant spelling patterns. The comparison concerns their pronunciations, not similarities in their meanings.

blocks.text: **Sublexical information concerns units smaller than a whole word.** Rapid nonword reading and the advantage for typical spelling–sound patterns show that readers use this information. **Lexical information** concerns knowledge of particular words. A complete account must explain how experience with a specific word contributes alongside general spelling patterns.

**General decoding explains part of reading, but familiar-word knowledge also needs an account.** The two sources of information are conceptually distinguishable even before deciding how they are implemented.
children: Nonwords test generalization, while differences among familiar words can reveal word-specific knowledge. These are evidence types, not proof that two independent modules must exist.

blocks.text: **Word knowledge can help identify an ambiguous letter.** In an interactive activation network, visual features activate letters and letters activate candidate words. Activated word candidates send feedback to their constituent letters. A letter supported by a plausible word receives additional activation even when its local visual evidence is unclear.
children: Competing candidates do not remain equally active. Their activation changes as the network settles on an interpretation.

blocks.text: **Letter recognition can depend on the word surrounding the letter.** Feedback supplies a mechanism by which whole-word knowledge influences perception.
children: The network links features, letters and words. The letter-output graph shows one candidate increasing while competing candidates remain low, illustrating a developing preference rather than instantaneous recognition.

blocks.text: **Feedback carries word-level activation back to letters.** A partially activated known word increases activation of the letters that belong to it. This makes recognition interactive. Information does not flow only from isolated features upward to a finished word.
children: The mechanism helps explain why an ambiguous letter can become easier to recognize when it appears in a familiar word context.

blocks.text: **Recognizing a word and recognizing its letters can support one another.** Top-down feedback is the word-to-letter part of that interaction.
children: The direction of a connection matters. Letter-to-word activation provides evidence for a candidate, while word-to-letter feedback supports the candidate's components.

blocks.text: **Lexicality and word frequency reveal effects of word-specific experience.** Real words are generally named faster than pseudowords, and frequently encountered words are named faster than less frequent words. Lexicality compares whether the item is a word. Frequency compares how often a particular word has been encountered.
children: The English Lexicon Project data show that the frequency effect occurs across many observations, rather than depending on a few unusually easy examples.

blocks.text: **Familiarity with a particular word contributes to reading speed.** Knowing general spelling patterns does not remove the benefit of repeated encounters with that word.
children: A frequency effect is a relation between prior exposure and naming performance. It is not the claim that all high-frequency words have the same length or pronunciation pattern.

blocks.text: **Multiple regression tests whether frequency predicts reading time after accounting for other word properties.** Length and sound-related characteristics could otherwise be mistaken for effects of frequency. The analysis uses about 3,000 words read by young and older adults. Frequency still contributes when other predictors are considered.
children: This makes a simple length-confound explanation less plausible. It does not turn an observational predictor into an experimentally isolated cause.

blocks.text: **The frequency effect is not adequately explained by saying that frequent words are merely shorter.** Its contribution survives statistical control of other properties.
children: The highlighted objective- and subjective-frequency coefficients are negative. Higher frequency is associated with shorter reaction times, with separate columns for lexical decision and naming in the two age groups.

blocks.text: **Frequency and regularity interact.** Low-frequency exception words are slowed much more than low-frequency regular words, whereas high-frequency words show a much smaller regularity difference. Naming latency is the time needed to begin saying the word. Higher values mean slower responses.
children: An interaction means the effect of one factor depends on the other. The regularity cost is not a fixed amount added equally to high- and low-frequency words.

blocks.text: **Experience matters especially when pronunciation conflicts with the usual spelling pattern.** Frequent exposure reduces the disadvantage of exception words.
children: The lines are close at high frequency and separate at low frequency. Exception words rise to roughly 580 ms, while regular words rise only to roughly 555 ms in this figure.

blocks.text: **A dual-route interpretation separates lexical retrieval from sublexical decoding.** The lexical process supplies the learned pronunciation of a particular word, while decoding computes pronunciation from spelling units. For a high-frequency word, lexical information becomes available quickly enough to reduce the influence of the decoding output.
children: For a low-frequency exception, the lexical response is less efficient and the regularized decoding output can interfere. Nonwords depend on decoding because they lack a stored whole-word entry.

blocks.text: **Two routes can explain why regularity matters most for unfamiliar words.** Fast lexical processing protects familiar exceptions from competing sublexical output.
children: This is an interpretation of the interaction, not the interaction itself. Other architectures must be evaluated against the same observed pattern.

blocks.text: **Acquired phonological dyslexia involves disproportionate difficulty reading pseudowords after brain injury.** Familiar words can remain relatively well read even when novel forms are difficult. Cacciopo van Vliet and colleagues compare real-word reading with several nonword tasks. The patients can often recognize and pronounce known words while struggling to generate a plausible pronunciation for an unfamiliar spelling.
children: The selective difficulty suggests that familiar-word success and novel-form decoding do not rely on every process to the same degree.

blocks.text: **Preserved word reading does not guarantee preserved decoding.** A patient can draw on learned word information while performing poorly on novel letter sequences.
children: The real-word table contains many high accuracy values, while several nonword lists have much lower scores. The deficit is relative, not a claim that every nonword response is wrong.

blocks.text: **Acquired surface dyslexia involves disproportionate difficulty reading irregular words after brain injury.** Errors often regularize the word by applying a more common spelling–sound pattern. DEAF pronounced like “deef” and SHOE pronounced like “show” illustrate regularization. The response is related to the spelling, but it is not the target word's learned pronunciation.
children: Relatively good regular-word and nonword reading shows that generating pronunciation from spelling can remain useful despite difficulty with exceptions.

blocks.text: **Surface dyslexia exposes the cost of relying on typical correspondences when a word is exceptional.** The errors are systematic rather than arbitrary failures to see the letters.
children: HFR and LFR refer to high- and low-frequency regular words. HFE and LFE refer to exceptions. The highlighted exception columns are lower, especially for low-frequency exceptions.

blocks.text: **A double dissociation compares opposite relative impairments.** Phonological dyslexia particularly affects pseudowords, while surface dyslexia particularly affects exception words. The first pattern shows that unfamiliar decoding can be difficult despite relatively preserved familiar-word reading. The second shows that exception reading can be difficult despite relatively preserved pseudoword reading.
children: Together, the patterns are harder to explain by saying that one task is simply harder for everyone.

blocks.text: **Opposite patient patterns support separable contributions to reading.** They are stronger evidence than a single group doing worse on one difficult task.
children: “Relatively spared” does not mean perfect. The inference concerns the difference between task profiles, not an absence of every error in the better-performing condition.

blocks.text: **A double dissociation challenges a single fixed difficulty ranking.** If task A were merely harder than task B, damage might consistently hurt A more, but it would not readily explain another patient showing the reverse pattern. The reversal suggests that the tasks depend differently on underlying processes. For reading, pseudowords and exception words place different demands on the system.
children: The evidence still requires a theory of what those underlying processes are. It does not uniquely identify a particular set of boxes in a model.

blocks.text: **The strength of a double dissociation comes from the reversal across cases.** The interpretation must explain both directions of impairment.
children: Compare the relative task costs within each patient or group, then compare those profiles. Two low scores without an opposite pattern are not a double dissociation.

blocks.text: **A dual-route model attributes phonological dyslexia to damage in grapheme–phoneme conversion and surface dyslexia to damage in lexical processing.** These proposed locations connect the task dissociation to specific mechanisms. Damage to conversion particularly affects nonwords because there is no familiar whole-word pronunciation to retrieve.
children: Damage to input or output word representations, called logogens in this account, or their connections makes exceptions vulnerable because general decoding supplies the wrong pronunciation.

blocks.text: **The model turns an observed dissociation into a claim about damaged processing components.** Each proposed lesion must produce the corresponding pattern of spared and impaired performance.
children: The lexical and conversion paths are theoretical components. Their labels should not be confused with a direct anatomical map of two single brain regions.

blocks.text: **Patterson's discussion shows why reading errors can complicate a clean lexical–nonlexical division.** Errors attributed to a purely nonlexical route can still show lexical influences. The example “incense” read as “increase” is a real-word response. A simple letter–sound mistake could instead produce a nonword, so the actual response raises a question about whole-word influence.
children: Possible responses are to allow a more complicated combination of routes or to revise the supposedly nonlexical process itself. The observation motivates refinement rather than settling the issue alone.

blocks.text: **A patient's error type matters as well as overall accuracy.** Lexical-looking errors challenge the idea that the remaining reading process is wholly independent of word knowledge.
children: The highlighted passage presents two alternatives for interpreting lexical influence in surface dyslexia. It does not simply declare that the patient evidence is irrelevant.

blocks.text: **Dual-route models distinguish a lexical route from a sublexical route.** Lexical processing uses knowledge of particular words, while grapheme–phoneme conversion generates pronunciation from spelling units. A model must explain fast pseudoword reading, faster familiar-word reading, frequency effects, regularity effects and their interaction.
children: It must also explain why pseudoword and exception-word reading can be differently impaired after brain injury. These observations motivate the architecture but do not uniquely prove it.

blocks.text: **The two-route proposal connects several reading findings to a common processing account.** Its success depends on explaining the full pattern, not only nonword reading.
children: A grapheme is a written unit associated with a sound. The route labels specify kinds of information used during reading.

blocks.text: **The Dual Route Cascaded model, or DRC, combines interactive lexical processing with a separate grapheme–phoneme rule system.** The two routes can contribute activation toward a spoken response. The lexical portion includes orthographic and phonological lexicons, representing written and spoken word forms. These representations are distinguished from meanings.
children: The implementation described here does not implement semantics. The GPC rule system also has processing assumptions different from those of the interactive lexical network.

blocks.text: **The DRC does not treat every connection as the same kind of computation.** Word-form activation and rule-based conversion are separate mechanisms.
children: The circled part of the diagram corresponds to interactive activation. The separate GPC path joins the output system rather than becoming another interactive lexical layer.

blocks.text: **The DRC's grapheme–phoneme conversion rules operate serially, letter by letter.** Their operation is not adjusted by word frequency and receives no lexical feedback. The GPC and lexical routes do not interact throughout their internal computations. They converge in the phoneme response buffer.
children: If the routes favor different phonemes, they can compete at that shared output. An exception word can therefore receive a correct lexical pronunciation and an incompatible regularized pronunciation.

blocks.text: **Encapsulation does not mean that the routes never affect the same response.** They remain separate internally but meet at the phoneme output.
children: Follow the route to the response buffer. Shared output units explain how competing pronunciations can influence naming even without feedback into the GPC rules.

blocks.text: **GPC rules map written units onto phonemes.** Some rules concern individual letters, while others concern several letters or a particular letter context. A model also needs a way to decide which applicable rule takes priority. A larger-unit rule can supersede rules for its individual letters.
children: Context-sensitive rules restrict a pronunciation to specified surrounding letters or positions. This makes the procedure more than a simple lookup of one sound per letter.

blocks.text: **A rule list is incomplete without a procedure for resolving overlapping rules.** Both the mapping and its conditions of application matter.
children: The table distinguishes multiletter rules from context-sensitive rules. Position labels specify whether a mapping applies at the beginning, middle, end or all positions.

blocks.text: **A categorical rule does not express the strength of the evidence behind it.** The DRC can choose a mapping because it is frequent, yet treat that mapping as a fixed rule during processing. The possible pronunciations of OUGH have more divided statistical support than those of EIGH. A rule can still operate categorically for both spellings.
children: A probabilistic account instead allows alternatives to receive different strengths of support. The distinction concerns processing, not whether the model designer ever consulted frequency information.

blocks.text: **Using statistics to select a rule differs from representing graded statistics while reading.** The two approaches can make different predictions for ambiguous spellings.
children: The table distributes pronunciation frequencies across alternatives. A spread across many rows indicates greater uncertainty than a distribution concentrated on one pronunciation.

blocks.text: **The DRC's simple rules are intended to explain systematic human errors as well as correct reading.** More finely tuned rules might pronounce more exceptions correctly but remove behavior the model is meant to explain. A regularizing route helps account for errors in surface dyslexia and for slow naming of low-frequency exception words.
children: The theory therefore claims that people's sublexical computation is constrained, rather than assuming that the best possible spelling algorithm is the correct cognitive model.

blocks.text: **A cognitively useful model should reproduce the relevant failures.** Maximizing pronunciation accuracy is not the only goal.
children: The crucial test is whether the same processing assumptions produce the observed pattern of success, interference and regularization, rather than an isolated incorrect response.

blocks.text: **Informational encapsulation means that a process does not freely use every source of relevant knowledge.** In the dual-route account, GPC conversion proceeds without consulting whole-word meaning or lexical feedback. This resembles a modular parsing proposal in which an early syntactic process follows structural principles without immediately using world knowledge.
children: Pseudoword naming exposes the conversion procedure because a familiar lexical entry is unavailable. Regularization errors expose it when conversion favors the wrong pronunciation.

blocks.text: **A modular account predicts restricted access to information.** The GPC route may produce an inappropriate response even when another part of the system has word-specific knowledge.
children: The comparison with parsing concerns processing restrictions. It does not mean that syntactic parsing and letter–sound conversion use the same representations.

blocks.text: **The DRC is evaluated against many reading phenomena.** These include frequency, lexicality, regularity, interactions, lexical decision and patterns in acquired dyslexia. Accounting for several effects with one architecture is stronger than fitting a single result. It also requires examining which assumptions stay fixed and which are changed between tasks.
children: The model's research strategy places strong weight on human behavioral evidence as a constraint on architecture.

blocks.text: **A broad list of successful simulations is informative, but the conditions of each success also matter.** Model evaluation includes both coverage and the assumptions used to obtain it.
children: The listed effects span reading aloud, lexical decision and patient performance. These are related but distinct tasks, so a task-specific adjustment must be identified as such.

blocks.text: **Lexical decision requires deciding whether a written item is a word.** The DRC simulation adds decision criteria to the activation produced by its recognition system. A “yes” response can depend on a strongly activated single word or on total activity across the orthographic lexicon. A “no” response occurs if the criteria are not met by a deadline.
children: The implementation also changes inhibition and uses time-dependent thresholds. These choices help obtain a fit, but they add assumptions beyond the basic two-route diagram.

blocks.text: **Fitting lexical decision requires an account of the decision itself.** Recognition activity does not automatically specify when to say yes or no.
children: The thresholds and cycle deadlines implement response rules. Their conceptual role is more important here than memorizing each numerical cutoff.

blocks.text: **The DRC routes are modular in several related senses.** They use different processing assumptions, restrict information exchange and accept particular kinds of input. The GPC system takes letters as input and sends phoneme activation toward the response system. This is **domain specificity** in the account.
children: The absence of lexical feedback into the GPC system is **informational encapsulation**. Having two pathways alone would not establish those stronger restrictions.

blocks.text: **Modularity is a claim about how components operate and communicate.** It is more specific than drawing two arrows in a model.
children: Distinguish the restrictions on inputs, the rules of computation and the restrictions on communication. These are separate properties of the proposed architecture.

blocks.text: **PDP models treat reading as learned mappings among orthography, phonology and semantics.** Orthography is spelling, phonology is sound structure, and semantics is meaning. Seidenberg and McClelland trained an associative network to map spelling onto pronunciation. The modeled spelling-to-sound pathway used one learned mapping for different kinds of words.
children: Reading skill emerges from learning rather than being specified entirely as a hand-built list of rules and lexical entries.

blocks.text: **An emergentist account asks how experience creates useful reading behavior.** Regularity can arise from learning across words rather than from a separate rule mechanism.
children: The triangle's labels identify representational domains. A connection between domains represents a learned mapping, not an additional stored dictionary for every item.

blocks.text: **In a PDP account, rules are generalizations learned across words.** Whole-word knowledge is distributed across learned mappings instead of being stored only in a distinct lexical route. The same learning mechanism can capture both patterns shared by many words and information specific to a familiar word.
children: The research strategy asks whether domain-general learning can explain reading. This contrasts with choosing separate adult processing components primarily from neuropsychological dissociations.

blocks.text: **Word-specific knowledge and generalization can coexist in the same learned system.** They do not have to be implemented as a dictionary and a separate symbolic rule list.
children: “Distributed” refers to how knowledge is represented across the network. It does not mean that the model has no memory of individual words.

blocks.text: **A learned network can produce a frequency-by-regularity interaction without separate frequency and rule mechanisms.** Regular words receive support from patterns shared across many words. An exception conflicts with those patterns, so learning its particular mapping is especially important. Frequent exposure strengthens that word-specific mapping.
children: A low-frequency exception has both weak item-specific learning and poor support from the dominant pattern. This combination creates a larger disadvantage than either factor alone.

blocks.text: **Consistency supplies support from other words, while frequency strengthens experience with the particular word.** Their joint influence explains why infrequent exceptions are especially difficult.
children: The interaction is shared evidence that both architectures must explain. Producing it does not by itself establish whether the implementation contains symbolic rules.

blocks.text: **Consistency describes how many similar spellings support a pronunciation.** “Friends” have the relevant spelling pattern and a compatible pronunciation, while “enemies” support a competing pronunciation. LATE and DUST illustrate consistent patterns. GAVE and MINT have many friends but also enemies such as HAVE and PINT.
children: DOWN versus KNOWN and POUR versus SOUR illustrate ambiguity. An exception such as PINT has relatively little support compared with its competing neighborhood.

blocks.text: **Spelling–sound support varies in degree.** A statistical description captures differences that a simple regular-versus-irregular label can hide.
children: Friend and enemy are labels for pronunciation relations among similar spellings. They do not refer to semantic relationships between the words.

blocks.text: **A PDP model can pronounce nonwords using the weights learned from real words.** A new spelling activates patterns that overlap with familiar spellings, allowing the network to generalize. No stored entry for the particular nonword is required. The same learned correspondences that support consistent words can support a new combination.
children: This is a proposed mechanism for decoding without a separate GPC rule module.

blocks.text: **Novel pronunciation can result from applying learned statistical structure.** Nonword reading therefore does not automatically establish a separate symbolic route.
children: The relevant comparison is whether one learned mapping can handle both familiar words and new items. The claim must still be checked against the model's actual performance.

blocks.text: **Poor nonword performance can challenge either a theoretical proposal or a particular implementation.** The early model's nonword accuracy was weaker than desired. One possibility is that a single associative mechanism cannot explain the task. Another is that the chosen representations fail to capture the similarities needed for generalization.
children: Improving the implementation while retaining the theoretical mechanism helps distinguish these possibilities.

blocks.text: **A failed simulation does not identify its own cause.** The failure must be traced to the architecture, learning assumptions, representations or other implementation choices.
children: The important question is what changes when the model is repaired. A representational improvement is a different theoretical move from adding a separate nonword route.

blocks.text: **Generalization depends on how sound similarity is represented.** The early Seidenberg–McClelland model used Wickelfeatures, whose representation of phonology was problematic for nonword reading. Plaut and colleagues improved the phonological representations and obtained better nonword performance. This supports a representational explanation for at least part of the earlier failure.
children: Behavioral relations between phonological processing and decoding also make phonology a relevant target for explanation.

blocks.text: **Changing the representation can improve decoding without adding a symbolic rule system.** That distinction matters when evaluating the original theoretical claim.
children: The comparison concerns models with different representations. Better performance after that change is evidence about implementation, not proof that every associative model will succeed.

blocks.text: **A network generalizes through similarity.** If its phonological representation poorly captures similarities among words, the learned mapping cannot transfer as effectively to new forms. A familiar word can retain support from its own training history. A nonword lacks that item-specific experience and depends more heavily on generalization.
children: This produces a reason for unfamiliar forms to be especially vulnerable to poor representations without requiring a dedicated nonword mechanism.

blocks.text: **The same representational weakness can have unequal effects on words and nonwords.** Familiarity can partly compensate where new-item generalization cannot.
children: Distinguish a weaker shared representation from damage to a separate route. Both can create a task difference, but they locate the explanation differently.

blocks.text: **Harm and Seidenberg manipulated noise in phonological representations.** Increasing noise makes the sound representations less reliable while keeping the model's general learning framework. The manipulation produced poorer nonword decoding and relative sparing of word recognition. It also linked the severity of the phonological deficit to the degree of decoding difficulty.
children: The model therefore connects a reading pattern to the quality of a more general phonological system.

blocks.text: **A selective-looking reading deficit can emerge from degraded shared representations.** Nonwords are especially dependent on reliable generalization.
children: Noise is the manipulated model property. Word and nonword performance are outcomes, so the simulation tests a directional mechanistic proposal rather than merely observing a correlation.

blocks.text: **Damaging semantic support in a triangle model can impair exception-word reading especially strongly.** Plaut and colleagues added a simplified semantic contribution and examined what happened when it was lesioned. An exception has weak support from typical spelling–sound regularities. Meaning-related support can help produce its learned pronunciation.
children: Reducing that support creates a surface-dyslexia-like pattern without defining a separate exception-word list as the sole explanation.

blocks.text: **The model links exception reading to semantic processing.** A reading dissociation can reflect unequal dependence on broader language systems.
children: “Lesion” here means a controlled change to the computational model. It is distinct from directly observing where a particular patient's brain injury occurred.

blocks.text: **The triangle model's pathways share graded learning assumptions and interact during learning.** Semantic representations are directly involved rather than replaced by a lexicon defined as independent of meaning. Spelling-to-sound learning develops in the presence of meaning-related support. The contribution of one pathway therefore affects what another pathway learns.
children: This allows graded impairments. Phonological dyslexics can make some exception errors, and surface dyslexics can make some nonword errors.

blocks.text: **Multiple pathways do not necessarily imply modular routes.** Their learning rules, information types and interactions distinguish the accounts.
children: O denotes orthography, P phonology and S semantics. O-to-P and S-to-P mappings use the same general probabilistic assumptions, unlike DRC's distinct GPC and lexical procedures.

blocks.text: **Woollams and colleagues tested the predicted association between semantic ability and exception-word reading.** Lower semantic scores were associated with poorer low-frequency exception reading in patients with semantic dementia. The model and patient panels show comparable overall relationships, although individual patients vary. This supports an association between meaning and exceptional pronunciation.
children: The finding is informative because it links a reading weakness to a broader semantic measure rather than describing only a reading-task dissociation.

blocks.text: **The triangle account predicts that exception reading should vary with semantic ability.** The patient data broadly follow that relationship.
children: The semantic score decreases from left to right on the patient plot. The downward slope therefore means that poorer semantics goes with poorer reading, not that better semantics harms reading.

blocks.text: **Some patients have relatively good exception reading despite low semantic scores.** These cases challenge a perfect one-to-one relationship, but an account of graded association does not predict zero variability. Woollams and colleagues interpret such observations in relation to the full distribution rather than treating each outlier as an automatic refutation.
children: The scientific issue is whether the unusual cases show a stable separate pattern or arise within a noisy overall association.

blocks.text: **An outlier and a clean dissociation are not automatically the same thing.** The strength and reliability of the apparent exception matter.
children: Points above the horizontal reference line and left of the specified vertical boundary are singled out as unusual. Evaluate their location relative to the broader patient cloud and repeated measurements.

blocks.text: **Longitudinal observations track whether semantic and reading abilities change together within a patient.** Because semantic dementia progresses, repeated testing can reveal a trajectory rather than a single unusual score. In most cases, declining semantic ability accompanies declining exception-word reading. Some initially unusual observations move closer to the broader relation on retesting.
children: This strengthens the association while leaving room for variability between individuals.

blocks.text: **Repeated observations help test whether an apparent dissociation persists.** A one-time exceptional score is less compelling if the patient's later trajectory follows the general relation.
children: Lines connect observations from the same person. Movement toward lower semantic scores and lower reading accuracy shows coupled decline rather than a comparison of unrelated people only.

blocks.text: **Coltheart and colleagues generated 40,000 model patients with different lexical-route and GPC impairment levels.** For each real patient, they selected the model run that best matched the observed data. This produced an excellent fit to the patient scores. The selection procedure is part of how that fit was achieved.
children: The fit should be distinguished from predicting each patient's pattern before choosing among many possible parameter combinations.

blocks.text: **A flexible model can closely reproduce observed data.** Evaluating the explanation also requires asking how the matching simulation was selected.
children: The plotted patient and model lines lie close together. That visual agreement describes goodness of fit, while the large search over simulated patients describes flexibility.

blocks.text: **A better fit can be less informative if it relies on much greater flexibility.** Selecting the best match from many parameter combinations can reproduce a dataset without strongly constraining the underlying explanation. The question is not whether close agreement is bad in itself. It is whether the account predicts the relation with principled assumptions or accommodates each case after seeing the outcome.
children: Comparing theories therefore requires attention to both fit and how much freedom produced it.

blocks.text: **Goodness of fit is only one part of model evaluation.** A model should explain why the pattern occurs, not only contain a setting that resembles it.
children: The contrast is between constrained prediction and flexible post hoc matching. It does not justify rejecting a model merely because its numerical fit is strong.

blocks.text: **Dual-route and triangle models address many of the same findings.** Both must explain rapid nonword decoding, exception difficulty, the frequency–regularity interaction and acquired reading dissociations. Agreement on the phenomena does not mean agreement on mechanisms. One account emphasizes specialized routes, while the other emphasizes learning across interacting representational systems.
**The models compete over explanation, not over whether these basic reading patterns exist.** Shared behavioral success makes their differing assumptions especially important.
children: A useful comparison holds the phenomenon constant and asks what each model changes or computes to produce it.

blocks.text: **DRC attributes nonword decoding and regularity effects to GPC rules, while the triangle account attributes them to statistical learning.** Word-specific exposure strengthens learned mappings in the triangle account and affects lexical processing in DRC. For phonological dyslexia, DRC emphasizes GPC damage and the triangle account emphasizes broader phonological impairment.
children: For surface dyslexia, DRC emphasizes lexical-route damage and the triangle account emphasizes semantic impairment.

blocks.text: **The same task pattern receives a different mechanistic explanation in each model.** Keep the observed phenomenon separate from the proposed locus of impairment.
children: Read each table row across the two model columns. The row identifies the finding, while the columns specify competing explanations rather than two names for identical components.

blocks.text: **A major contrast is whether the explanation begins with separate reading routes or broader language associations.** Dual-route models use different task impairments to motivate independent processes. The statistical-learning account links phonology to spelling–sound generalization and semantics to words whose pronunciation is poorly supported by that generalization.
children: Both dissociations and associations matter. A theory should explain selective weaknesses and the related abilities that vary with them.

blocks.text: **Phonological and semantic measures can help identify what lies behind a reading dissociation.** They extend the evidence beyond the reading scores alone.
children: The table's dyslexia rows contrast GPC versus phonological damage and lexical-route versus semantic damage. These are the key theoretical alternatives, not just different diagnostic labels.

blocks.text: **Morphology is generative because speakers can form words they have not memorized individually.** Derivational morphology creates a new lexical form, while inflection marks grammatical information such as plural or past tense. The central question is how a speaker extends a familiar pattern to a new item. English plural and past-tense formation provide tractable examples.
children: Generalization can also produce playful or incorrect forms. This shows productive use of patterns, rather than a vocabulary containing only previously heard responses.

blocks.text: **Productive word formation goes beyond retrieving a stored list.** The theoretical issue is whether that productivity requires symbolic rules or can emerge from learning.
children: The playful “crew” and “crode” examples extend irregular-sounding patterns to CRY. They demonstrate creative generalization, not correct standard English past-tense forms.

blocks.text: **Berko Gleason's wug test measures morphological generalization to a novel word.** A child learns a new label and then supplies an inflected form that has not been provided. The pictured task introduces one WUG and then asks about two. Producing WUGS applies plural knowledge to a new noun.
children: The same logic can test past tense using novel verbs. Success shows productive knowledge, but does not by itself distinguish symbolic rules from statistical generalization.

blocks.text: **A novel item prevents success from being explained as retrieval of that item's memorized inflection.** The child must extend a learned pattern.
children: The drawing depicts plural formation, even though the accompanying discussion also mentions past tense. Keep the displayed plural task separate from the broader application of the method.

blocks.text: **Regular past tense follows the productive -ed pattern.** SHOW becomes SHOWED, BAKE becomes BAKED, and a novel verb such as BLICK can become BLICKED. Irregular pairs such as GO–WENT, TAKE–TOOK and EAT–ATE do not follow that default form. Some irregulars share smaller patterns with other verbs.
children: A theory must explain both familiar exceptions and productive extension to novel verbs.

blocks.text: **Past-tense knowledge includes generalization and item-specific variation.** The contrast creates a test for different theories of morphology.
children: Compare regular real verbs with regularized nonwords, then with learned irregular pairs. The nonwords test extension, while the irregulars test successful handling of exceptions.

blocks.text: **The Words and Rules account gives regular and irregular inflection different mechanisms.** A symbolic rule generates a regular past tense, while irregular forms are stored in an associative lexical system. The regular process can apply to a new verb because it does not require an entry for that particular past tense.
children: The irregular system stores word-specific information and can be influenced by frequency and similarity. A successful explanation also needs to prevent an available irregular form from being replaced by a regularization.

blocks.text: **In this account, productive rule application and remembered exceptions are separate kinds of knowledge.** That is stronger than simply observing that regular and irregular forms look different.
children: “Add -ed” summarizes the symbolic operation. The associative system is not proposed as another copy of the same rule.

blocks.text: **The lexicon and grammar offer different ways to produce a past tense.** Lexical retrieval supplies an irregular form such as HELD, while grammatical combination can produce WALK plus -ed. Pinker and Ullman's diagram associates lexical lookup with declarative memory and grammatical combination with procedural processing.
children: Like dual-route reading, the account separates word-specific knowledge from a productive operation. Unlike reading aloud, its task is to transform a stem according to a grammatical feature, rather than convert spelling into sound.

blocks.text: **Similar-looking architectures can solve different computational problems.** Keep morphological inflection separate from grapheme–phoneme conversion.
children: The input includes a stem and a past-tense feature. The diagram distinguishes lexical association from combination, and its blocking connection prevents a retrieved irregular from competing unchecked with a regular form.

blocks.text: **The Words and Rules proposal was motivated partly by a theory of grammar.** A categorical symbolic grammar describes productive patterns, but language also contains exceptions. Reading dual-route theories were strongly motivated by neuropsychological dissociations. The morphology proposal also reflects a commitment to keeping the grammatical rule system distinct from exceptional lexical information.
**The motivation for an architecture matters when evaluating its evidence.** Similar diagrams do not mean that the theories were derived from the same observations.
children: The contrast is between a dissociation-driven reading account and a grammatical argument for separating productive rules from exceptions.

blocks.text: **An associative lexicon handles information that does not fit a categorical rule.** Its representations are word-specific and sensitive to frequency and phonological similarity. KEEP–KEPT, WEEP–WEPT and LEAP–LEAPT illustrate similarity among irregular forms. An exception can belong to a small family rather than being wholly unrelated to other words.
children: Assigning these properties to lexical memory lets the rule system remain categorical and general.

blocks.text: **Separating exceptions protects a simple rule, but creates a second mechanism that must also be explained.** The associative system carries graded and item-specific influences.
children: The shared sound pattern in the listed verbs motivates associative similarity. It is not evidence that every irregular verb uses exactly the same transformation.

blocks.text: **Rumelhart and McClelland modeled past tense as a learned association between present and past sound patterns.** A single trainable network learns across verbs instead of applying a separately specified -ed rule. The model encodes a root's phonology, transforms that representation through modifiable connections, and decodes an output pattern.
children: Regularity is a pattern learned from many examples. Irregular forms are also learned within the same system.

blocks.text: **One learning mechanism is proposed for both regularities and exceptions.** The challenge is to explain accurate generalization as well as familiar forms.
children: The fixed encoding and decoding stages surround a modifiable pattern associator. Wickelfeatures represent sound patterns, while the trainable connections store the learned mapping.

blocks.text: **U-shaped learning describes an initial success, a decline, and later recovery.** A child may correctly say RAN, later produce RUNNED, and eventually return to RAN. The middle error is a **regularization**, because the child applies the common past-tense pattern to an irregular verb.
children: The decline does not necessarily mean that the child has stopped learning. A changing system can generalize more broadly while temporarily disrupting an earlier correct response.

blocks.text: **Development can involve temporary errors as knowledge changes.** A theory must explain the entire trajectory, not just the final adult response.
children: The vertical dimension is successful performance and the horizontal dimension is development or training. A U shape concerns accuracy over time, not the shape of a word.

blocks.text: **The Words and Rules account explains U-shaped learning through changes in the use of rules and lexical exceptions.** Early correct forms can be imitated before a productive rule is available. When the rule is learned, it can be applied too broadly, yielding RUNNED. Later, learned irregulars and the blocking process prevent that regularization.
children: This account treats the developmental stages as involving distinguishable processes rather than only gradual changes in one mapping.

blocks.text: **Overregularization is interpreted as productive rule use that is not yet sufficiently constrained by exceptions.** Recovery depends on the irregular form winning over the rule output.
children: Blocking means that retrieval of the appropriate irregular prevents the otherwise available regular form. It is a proposed mechanism, not merely another name for correct performance.

blocks.text: **Changing the training vocabulary can produce U-shaped learning in one network.** Early training emphasizes frequent irregular verbs, allowing those particular mappings to be learned. As more regular verbs enter training, their common pattern changes the network's responses. That generalization can interfere with previously learned irregulars.
children: With further learning, the network can recover the irregular responses while retaining broad regularity. No new symbolic rule component is inserted at the point of decline.

blocks.text: **A shift in the distribution of experience can temporarily disrupt familiar responses.** The learning account explains the developmental pattern through changing weights and input.
children: The lower plot contrasts correct irregular responses with regularized alternatives. Their changing strengths illustrate competition during training, rather than the sudden appearance of a separate rule box.

blocks.text: **Testing untrained verbs asks whether the network learned transferable structure.** A real English verb can be novel to a model if it was excluded from that model's training set. The test therefore uses the logic of a wug task even when the items are real words to humans.
children: The model can generate many appropriate past-tense features, but feature-level success must be distinguished from producing an entirely correct word.

blocks.text: **Generalization is defined relative to the learner's experience.** A familiar human word is still a valid novel-model test when it was withheld from training.
children: The summary reports proportions of Wickelfeatures generated correctly. A high proportion of correct features does not imply that the same proportion of whole words was pronounced perfectly.

blocks.text: **Some model outputs contain changes that are unlike ordinary human regularizations.** Examples include MADE(D)-like changes to MATE and the unusual outputs MEMBLED for MAIL and TOUREDER for TOUR. The model authors acknowledge that people are unlikely to make some of these errors. They suggest that additional output constraints could reduce bizarre responses.
children: This separates capturing an overall learning pattern from matching the detailed form of human errors.

blocks.text: **A plausible learning curve is not enough if the model produces implausible words.** Error structure provides another test of the representation and decoding process.
children: The quotation discusses outputs near threshold and a possible cleanup mechanism. That proposed mechanism is an explanation to be tested, not a repair already demonstrated by the quoted result.

blocks.text: **Prince and Pinker argued that feature representations can blend distinct alternatives.** A model may activate features belonging to several possible past-tense forms without keeping those candidates separate. For SING, partial support for different sound patterns can overlap. Decoding the combined activation can produce a hybrid rather than selecting a coherent word.
children: The criticism targets the representation and its treatment of competing outputs, not merely the presence of learning.

blocks.text: **Combining evidence for alternatives is different from blending the alternatives into a new malformed output.** A model must preserve the distinctions needed to produce a coherent response.
children: The highlighted MEMBLED example makes the criticism concrete. It is presented as an unwanted hybrid, not as a normal past tense that children commonly produce.

blocks.text: **Joanisse and Seidenberg propose that phonology supports rule-like generalization while semantics especially supports irregular forms.** The same system links speech input, meaning and speech output. Reliable sound representations support extension from familiar present–past pairs to new forms. Irregular mappings receive additional support from the particular word's semantic representation.
children: The hypothesis concerns different degrees of dependence on shared systems, rather than a separate symbolic rule route for every regular response.

blocks.text: **The regular–irregular contrast can arise from how phonological and semantic information contribute.** A graded system can produce systematic differences between item types.
children: The diagram connects speech input and semantics through learned mappings to speech output. Its components represent domains of information, not a list of regular and irregular words in separate boxes.

blocks.text: **The model aims to explain the dissociation between irregular and nonword past-tense performance.** These tasks differ in how much they depend on learned word-specific information and phonological generalization. A nonword has no familiar item-specific semantic history to support its inflection. A known irregular can require semantic support because its output is not well predicted by the dominant pattern.
children: Manipulating phonological or semantic integrity tests whether these different dependencies can produce opposite impairment profiles.

blocks.text: **The same architecture should explain both sides of the patient pattern.** Selectivity must arise from the manipulated representations and their contribution to the task.
children: The target is a pattern of performance across item types. Drawing phonology and semantics in a diagram is not enough unless damaging them produces the relevant outcomes.

blocks.text: **The patient pattern associated here with Broca's aphasia includes especially poor nonword past-tense production.** These patients have left anterior injury and difficulty producing speech. Regular forms are also vulnerable, while irregular forms are relatively better in the displayed comparison. A novel BLICK must be transformed without relying on a familiar stored past tense.
children: This motivates investigating phonological contributions to the apparent morphological deficit.

blocks.text: **Difficulty with productive inflection may be connected to sound processing.** The nonword condition is particularly demanding because it relies on generalization.
children: The graph places nonword accuracy below regular and irregular accuracy. The irregular advantage over regulars is smaller than the nonword disadvantage, so these differences should not be treated as equally large.

blocks.text: **Phonological impairment reduces past-tense performance most strongly for nonwords in the model.** Regulars are numerically worse than irregulars, but the largest difference concerns novel forms. The model manipulation weakens sound-based computation. Familiar words retain support unavailable to an untrained nonword.
children: The similarity to the patient pattern shows how a selective-looking morphological deficit can arise from a broader phonological impairment.

blocks.text: **Damaging phonology can imitate a failure of productive morphology without removing a symbolic rule.** The mechanism being tested is the quality of sound representations.
children: Model and patient bars are paired within regular, irregular and nonword conditions. Compare the profile across conditions rather than expecting exact equality of every bar.

blocks.text: **Other patient groups show a larger problem with irregular past-tense forms.** The material discusses Wernicke's and Alzheimer's patients and anomic patients with inferior or middle temporal injury. Their irregular performance is lower than their regular and nonword performance in the displayed comparison.
children: This creates the other side of the dissociation and motivates examining the information that especially supports known irregular forms.

blocks.text: **Relatively preserved nonword inflection can coexist with poor irregular inflection.** The theory must explain this reverse pattern as well as phonological impairment.
children: The middle bar is the irregular condition, at roughly 60% correct, compared with higher regular and nonword scores. The diagnostic labels do not make every individual's performance identical.

blocks.text: **Semantic impairment particularly disrupts irregular past-tense forms.** When the model loses meaning-related support, irregular accuracy falls below regular and nonword accuracy. Typical phonological patterns still support many regular and novel forms. Nonwords can nevertheless be somewhat worse than regular words because they lack item-specific training.
children: This shows how unequal dependence on semantics can produce the reverse of the phonological-damage profile.

blocks.text: **Irregular vulnerability is predicted from its greater dependence on semantic support.** The model does not have to delete an isolated exception list to produce that pattern.
children: The irregular bars are the lowest for both the model and the comparison patients. The figure compares profiles, not a claim that model lesions reproduce every aspect of Alzheimer's disease.

blocks.text: **Phonological controls can change the apparent regular–irregular difference.** Bird and colleagues found that the difference in Broca's patients was reduced when items were adequately matched for phonology. Patterson and colleagues found that irregular impairment in semantic dementia correlated with semantic deficit severity.
children: These findings connect morphology to phonological and semantic abilities, making a pure rule-versus-word interpretation less straightforward.

blocks.text: **A task dissociation should be checked for differences in the demands of its items.** Related abilities can explain why one condition is more vulnerable.
children: Matching phonology addresses a potential confound in the regular–irregular comparison. Correlating semantic severity with irregular performance tests an association predicted by the alternative account.

blocks.text: **Phonological representations support learning the common mapping from present to past.** A degraded representation makes that generalization less reliable, especially for new words. Semantic information supports forms that depart from the dominant -ed pattern. Some irregulars also benefit from smaller phonological families and can be relatively spared.
children: Regularity and exception status therefore describe degrees of statistical support rather than perfectly isolated kinds of processing.

blocks.text: **Different forms draw on the same systems to different degrees.** General patterns and word-specific support can jointly determine an output.
children: The comparison with triangle reading concerns the division of support between phonology and semantics. Spelling-to-sound reading and present-to-past inflection remain different tasks.

blocks.text: **Specific language impairment, or SLI in the course terminology, involves impaired language development despite relatively typical nonverbal performance.** Difficulties can include morphology and syntax. The profile can also involve phonology, reading, working memory and speech perception. This broader range matters when evaluating a theory that locates the problem only in grammar.
children: A relative language difficulty does not by itself identify a single damaged learning mechanism.

blocks.text: **The diagnostic description and the causal explanation are separate.** A grammatical difficulty can coexist with weaknesses in other processes that support language.
children: The list extends beyond grammatical categories. Those additional domains are relevant evidence, not automatically irrelevant symptoms because the condition is called language impairment.

blocks.text: **A rule-deficit account predicts particular difficulty with regular and novel inflections.** If a domain-specific rule-learning mechanism is impaired, irregular forms stored lexically should be relatively less affected. This proposal uses past-tense performance to argue for a mechanism specific to grammatical rules.
children: The prediction must be tested against the complete pattern, including irregular performance and broader phonological difficulties.

blocks.text: **The crucial issue is whether the deficit is selective enough to support the proposed rule mechanism.** Merely finding poor past tense does not establish its cause.
children: Regular real words, irregular real words and nonwords are separate conditions. A theory should state how each condition is expected to change.

blocks.text: **The van der Lely and Ullman comparison shows low past-tense accuracy across all three item types in the SLI group.** Same-age controls perform much better. Nonwords are especially difficult for the SLI group, but regulars and irregulars are also impaired. The results therefore contain a broad deficit as well as unequal condition difficulty.
children: An explanation should account for the entire profile rather than reporting only that productive forms are poor.

blocks.text: **The observed pattern is broader than a simple intact-irregulars versus damaged-rules contrast.** Novel forms are most vulnerable, while familiar forms are not unaffected.
children: The SLI bars are approximately 20% for regulars, somewhat lower for irregulars and below 10% for nonwords. The controls' bars are much higher in all three categories.

blocks.text: **Weakening phonological processing produces impaired learning across forms, with nonwords especially vulnerable.** The severe and weaker impairment settings differ in the degree of difficulty. The intact model performs substantially better. Even intact learning shows different performance across regulars, irregulars and nonwords.
children: The comparison tests whether a phonological learning weakness can reproduce important aspects of the behavioral profile without a missing grammatical rule.

blocks.text: **A graded phonological manipulation creates graded developmental impairment.** Novel generalization is most fragile because it cannot rely on a word's own training history.
children: Compare severe phonology, weaker phonology and intact settings. The bars report percent correct, and the intact model is shown at two training points, so training amount and impairment should not be conflated.

blocks.text: **Phonology contributes to every spoken past-tense response.** Weakening it can therefore reduce performance on regulars, irregulars and nonwords. Nonwords are particularly dependent on generalizing a sound pattern to a new form. Familiar words have additional item-specific learning that can partly support their responses.
**An especially large nonword deficit does not imply that other forms avoid phonology.** It reflects different degrees of dependence on generalization.
children: The pattern to explain is broad impairment with a disproportionate nonword cost. A theory that predicts only one affected category misses part of that pattern.

blocks.text: **The associative account learns mappings among phonology and semantics without a separate symbolic past-tense rule or an isolated exception lexicon.** Regular and irregular are useful descriptions of behavior, but only approximate descriptions of the system's internal organization. Irregular performance is associated with semantic processing. Wug-test performance is associated with phonological processing.
children: These associations provide tests of the proposed underlying mechanisms, beyond simply assigning different item types to different boxes.

blocks.text: **Past-tense behavior can be explained through learned structure and unequal support from shared representations.** The proposal must still explain developmental, patient and generalization data together.
children: The contrast with Words and Rules concerns representation and computation, not whether the English language contains recognizable regular and irregular patterns.

blocks.text: **Linguistic relativity concerns whether differences in language influence how people organize or use concepts.** The Sapir and Whorf quotations suggest that linguistic categories can shape how experience is interpreted. The strongest reading would make language determine what a person can think. A weaker claim is that habitual language use biases attention, memory or preferred ways of representing a situation.
children: These claims require different evidence. A preference associated with language does not establish that alternative thought is impossible.

blocks.text: **Influencing thought is different from completely determining thought.** Keep that distinction explicit when interpreting a language-group difference.
children: The quotations express broad theoretical ideas. They are not experimental demonstrations that two speakers are unable to understand the same physical event.

blocks.text: **Language is embedded in cultural practices and experience.** A difference between language communities may therefore covary with factors other than linguistic structure. Sapir and Whorf should not automatically be assigned the strongest deterministic interpretation of selected quotations.
children: A precise study must identify which cognitive process is affected and what alternative explanations the comparison controls.

blocks.text: **Testing linguistic relativity requires a narrower claim than saying that every language creates a completely separate world.** Space and time provide specific domains in which to test representational preferences.
children: Historical framing explains why language and culture were often discussed together. It also highlights the need to distinguish their contributions in an experiment.

blocks.text: **A location description needs a frame of reference.** Saying where the ball is requires choosing what counts as left, front or a stable direction. The ball can be located with respect to the viewer, the chair's own orientation or a direction independent of either.
children: Different descriptions can identify the same physical position while organizing that position differently.

blocks.text: **The object does not have to move for its verbal description to change.** Changing the reference frame changes the relation being described.
children: The chair and ball are the meaningful stimuli. The question is which reference determines the ball's location, not a judgment about the objects' appearance.

blocks.text: **An intrinsic frame uses an object's own orientation, a relative frame uses an observer's viewpoint, and an absolute frame uses a stable direction.** These are different ways to specify the same location. “At the chair's front” uses the chair's intrinsic front. “To the left of the chair from my viewpoint” depends on the observer.
children: “North of the chair” uses an absolute direction that does not reverse when the observer turns around.

blocks.text: **Ask what fixes the direction in each description.** The object's orientation, the observer's body and a stable external direction are not interchangeable.
children: The ball–chair example holds the scene constant while changing the reference. Rotating the observer changes relative left and right but does not change north.

blocks.text: **Egocentric spatial descriptions use the speaker's position and orientation.** Left, right, in front and behind are familiar examples for nearby objects. Tzeltal commonly uses absolute directions in circumstances where English speakers might use these relative terms.
children: The contrast motivates asking whether habitual language use relates to nonverbal spatial coding, rather than merely comparing two ways of giving spoken directions.

blocks.text: **A direction can stay fixed when a person turns.** Absolute coding differs from coding an object as being on the viewer's left.
children: The language comparison concerns preferred spatial descriptions. It does not imply that speakers of either language are incapable of learning another frame.

blocks.text: **Tzeltal's uphill and downhill terms function as an absolute directional system.** Their historical connection to a slope does not mean that each use simply points to the nearest visible hill. A direction is retained as a stable spatial reference rather than being recalculated from the speaker's current left and right.
children: This allows positions to be described consistently as the speaker changes orientation.

blocks.text: **A landmark origin and an absolute use are different properties.** A historically landscape-based term can become a stable directional reference.
children: The contrast is with a description that depends entirely on the current viewpoint. The relevant feature is how the reference behaves across changes in location and orientation.

blocks.text: **A landmark-based direction is tied to a particular environment.** Uptown and downtown organize movement within Manhattan but do not provide a universally usable compass system. A city's conventional map orientation can also differ from magnetic north. Familiar spatial language therefore reflects local practices as well as geometric directions.
**A stable local convention is not automatically an absolute frame that transfers everywhere.** Its usefulness depends on the landmark system being available.
children: The Manhattan example distinguishes local orientation from cardinal direction. It is a contrast about reference systems rather than an experiment demonstrating linguistic causation.

blocks.text: **The chips task separates relative from absolute spatial memory by rotating the participant 180 degrees.** A participant sees a configuration, waits, and then chooses its match at a second table. A relative response preserves the arrangement with respect to the person's viewpoint. An absolute response preserves its orientation in the environment, so the two responses diverge after rotation.
children: Dutch speakers predominantly gave relative responses, while Tzeltal speakers gave more absolute responses. The association is consistent with their preferred linguistic frames but does not isolate language from all other experience.

blocks.text: **The rotation makes two otherwise similar descriptions predict different choices.** The nonverbal response reveals a preferred spatial coding strategy.
children: The north arrow stays fixed while the person changes orientation. Red bars represent relative choices and blue bars absolute choices, showing different response distributions across the two language groups.

blocks.text: **Spatial inference can combine relations learned in different displays.** Participants learn the relation between two objects, rotate to another display, and learn a second relation involving a shared object. They then place an object relative to another using the combined information. Relative and absolute coding lead to different placements because the person's orientation has changed.
children: Dutch and Tzeltal response patterns again differ in the direction associated with their preferred spatial frames.

blocks.text: **The task goes beyond reproducing one remembered arrangement.** It asks whether a frame is used when combining spatial relations to make an inference.
children: The cube appears in both learning displays, linking the cone and cylinder relations. The final placement distinguishes a viewer-relative inference from one preserving environmental direction.

blocks.text: **Testing conditions could contribute to the apparent language-group difference.** Li and Gleitman noted that Tzeltal participants had been tested with visible, familiar outdoor landmarks, unlike many laboratory participants. An environment with useful landmarks can encourage landmark-based coding. A windowless laboratory can make viewer-relative descriptions more convenient.
children: Manipulating landmark availability within English speakers tests whether the behavior can change without changing native language.

blocks.text: **A language comparison can be confounded with a setting comparison.** The environment must be considered before assigning the entire difference to linguistic structure.
children: The critical contrast is access to spatial cues, not simply the label “laboratory.” Windows, outdoor views and familiar surroundings can alter which references are useful.

blocks.text: **English speakers' preference for relative coding weakened when external landmarks were available.** They strongly preferred relative responses with the blinds down, but the preference was less pronounced with a street view or outdoors. The manipulation changes the spatial information available while keeping the language group the same.
children: This demonstrates that task context can influence the response. It challenges an explanation in which language alone fixes the chosen frame.

blocks.text: **Spatial strategy is sensitive to the testing environment.** A within-language change helps reveal a potential confound in a between-language comparison.
children: A reduced relative preference is not necessarily a complete switch to absolute coding. Describe the observed change in preference without exaggerating it into an all-or-none reversal.

blocks.text: **If language groups are tested under different conditions, their response difference may partly reflect those conditions.** Visible landmarks and familiarity can covary with native language in a cross-community study. A controlled comparison must separate the effect of the environment from any contribution of habitual linguistic coding.
children: Showing an environmental effect does not prove that language never matters. It limits what can be inferred from an uncontrolled comparison.

blocks.text: **The relevant question is what the study actually isolates.** A language-group effect can be real while its causal interpretation remains unsettled.
children: A confound is a factor that changes with the variable of interest and offers another explanation for the result. It is not merely any feature present in the experiment.

blocks.text: **Levinson and colleagues argued that the simplified task could make the experimenter's purpose too obvious.** Low memory demands and short time or distance between displays may encourage a deliberate strategy about rotation. Participants who infer what is being tested can alter their response for reasons different from habitual spatial coding.
children: The response therefore focuses on memory load and task transparency, rather than denying that landmarks can ever matter.
