blocks.text: **Changing a task can change the process it measures.** A landmark effect in an easy, transparent task may not settle how people habitually remember spatial relations.
children: The proposed alternative is a demand-characteristic explanation. Participants' interpretation of the experiment may influence the response independently of their normal coding preference.

blocks.text: **Levinson and colleagues retested Dutch students with four animals, a longer delay and greater distance between tables.** The extra item and delay increased memory demands, while the distance made the rotation manipulation less conspicuous. Under these conditions, the preference for relative coding remained.
children: The result suggests that the environmental effect depends on how the task is arranged, including how much memory and strategic inference it encourages.

blocks.text: **A relative preference can persist despite changes in the environment when the memory task is more demanding.** This narrows the conditions under which the landmark alternative explains behavior.
children: Each procedural change has a purpose. More animals and a longer delay tax memory, while separation of the tables reduces the salience of the rotation.

blocks.text: **A robust spatial-frame preference under memory demands does not automatically identify a purely spatial representation.** Remembering the task can recruit verbal strategies as well as spatial ones. The relative preference is reported when memory demands are substantial and the experimenter's interest is less obvious.
children: That pattern makes it important to ask how the sequence is stored during the delay, not only which direction is chosen at the end.

blocks.text: **The involvement of memory creates another mechanism to examine.** A task can be nonverbal in its response while still allowing verbal recoding internally.
children: The two conditions concern memory load and task transparency. They specify when the effect is robust, rather than proving that all other explanations have been eliminated.

blocks.text: **Participants might remember the animals as a verbal list such as “lion, tiger, bear.”** Reconstructing that sequence from left to right can produce a relative-looking response. This strategy would connect language to the task through working memory and ordering habits, rather than through an inability to represent absolute space.
children: The interpretation changes because the same choice can arise from different internal codes.

blocks.text: **A nonverbal task does not guarantee nonverbal processing.** Verbal recoding is a concrete alternative mechanism for the spatial-memory result.
children: The proposed list preserves order but does not explicitly preserve compass direction. Translating that order into a left-to-right display can mimic a spatial-frame preference.

blocks.text: **Metaphorical language expresses one kind of experience using terms from another.** Saying that an argument is not “cutting” describes its effectiveness rather than a literal action with a blade. Physical and spatial terms can therefore help express abstract relations. Time is especially useful for studying whether such linguistic habits are associated with nonlinguistic representations.
children: The question is empirical. Using a spatial phrase does not by itself prove that every thought about time has the same spatial format.

blocks.text: **An expression can be meaningful without being literal.** The study of time asks whether familiar spatial expressions also relate to cognitive processing.
children: The lyric is an example of metaphorical expression. It is not experimental evidence for a particular direction of causation between language and thought.

blocks.text: **English and Mandarin both use horizontal spatial language for time, but Mandarin also frequently uses vertical terms.** Earlier events can be described with an “up” term and later events with a “down” term. The linguistic contrast motivates testing whether speakers differ in the spatial organization they use during temporal tasks.
children: The existence of the expressions is the starting observation. A behavioral task is needed to investigate whether the contrast extends beyond words.

blocks.text: **Habitual ways of talking about time can suggest testable predictions about processing.** Mandarin's vertical terms make a vertical temporal organization a relevant possibility.
children: The examples contrast spatial and temporal uses of the same terms. “Up” in an expression for an earlier month is a temporal use, not a claim that the month occupies a physical location.

blocks.text: **Boroditsky's priming task tests whether spatial processing influences subsequent time judgments.** Participants first process horizontal or vertical relations, then respond to temporal earlier–later questions. English speakers respond faster after horizontal than vertical primes, while Mandarin speakers show the opposite pattern in the displayed comparison.
children: Training English speakers on vertical metaphors changes the pattern toward a vertical-prime advantage. This suggests sensitivity to experience, rather than an unchangeable division between language groups.

blocks.text: **The prime changes what representation is active before the temporal judgment.** Response-time differences reveal compatibility between the prime and the later task.
children: The vertical axis is reaction time, so a lower bar means faster processing. Compare horizontal and vertical bars within each group rather than interpreting the tallest bar as the best performance.

blocks.text: **Reading and writing habits can also organize sequences spatially.** Differences attributed to temporal metaphors may covary with whether text is commonly read left-to-right, right-to-left or vertically. Casasanto and Bottini use differences in text orientation and arrangement preferences to motivate this alternative.
children: The point is to identify another source of spatial experience, not to assume that a writing-system label perfectly predicts every individual's habits.

blocks.text: **Language-group differences can bundle linguistic and literacy experiences together.** Reading direction therefore needs to be measured or controlled.
children: The diagrams distinguish starting side and line direction. The table shows several arrangement patterns within the sampled groups, making individual experience relevant.

blocks.text: **Boroditsky and colleagues excluded Chinese readers who reported top-to-bottom reading.** This tests whether the vertical temporal effect can be explained entirely by that reported reading experience. English speakers show an advantage for a left-is-earlier horizontal mapping. Mandarin speakers also show an advantage for a top-is-earlier vertical mapping in the displayed comparison.
children: Retaining a vertical effect under this restriction weakens that particular reading-direction explanation, without proving that every possible experiential confound is removed.

blocks.text: **A targeted control tests a specific alternative explanation.** Its conclusion should be limited to the experience that was actually controlled.
children: White bars are canonical mappings and black bars noncanonical mappings. For vertical trials, canonical means top-is-earlier. Lower reaction times indicate a mapping advantage.

blocks.text: **Participants classify events as past or future using colored buttons.** The color-to-category mapping is reversed across blocks, so the past response is sometimes on the left and sometimes on the right. With standard text reading, responses are faster when past maps left and future maps right.
children: Because the response concerns time rather than an explicit judgment of spatial direction, the compatibility effect reveals an implicit spatial association in this task.

blocks.text: **Changing which side corresponds to past allows a direct test of spatial–temporal compatibility.** Color alone cannot explain the pattern because the mappings are counterbalanced.
children: The lower black bars represent the left-to-right temporal mapping. The effect concerns response time across mappings, not a change in which events count as past or future.

blocks.text: **Mirror reading tests whether short-term reading experience can alter spatial associations with time.** Participants read reversed text and perform the past–future button task. By the second mirror-reading block, the compatibility effect reverses. Responses are faster when earlier maps right and later maps left.
children: The result supports a contribution of reading-direction experience and shows that the association can change over a short period.

blocks.text: **A flexible temporal mapping is difficult to explain as a fixed consequence of native-language grammar alone.** Recent perceptual and reading experience contributes to performance.
children: The first block retains the usual advantage, while the second favors the opposite mapping. Compare the two colors within each block before comparing overall reaction times between blocks.

blocks.text: **Claims about a language's vocabulary are not automatically evidence for cognitive limits.** Pullum's discussion criticizes how an account of different word roots became an exaggerated story about language and thought. Languages can express distinctions through separate roots, derived words or phrases. Counting one of these forms without considering the others can misrepresent expressive capacity.
children: A reliable claim requires accurate linguistic description and an appropriate behavioral test, rather than repetition of a striking anecdote.

blocks.text: **Different lexical packaging does not show that one group cannot understand another group's distinctions.** The linguistic facts and the cognitive inference both need scrutiny.
children: The excerpt distinguishes roots from derivationally related forms and phrases. That distinction is central to why simple vocabulary counts can be misleading.

blocks.text: **A signed language is a natural language, while Braille is a writing system.** Signed languages have their own linguistic structure. Braille allows a language to be read through touch. The distinction matters because changing the modality of a language is not the same as changing how a written language is accessed.
children: Both cases reveal how sensory experience shapes the organization of systems involved in language and reading.

blocks.text: **Do not treat Braille as a signed language or signing as a tactile alphabet.** They provide different tests of language and neural plasticity.
children: The shared theme is modality, but the linguistic status of the two cases differs. A comparison should preserve that distinction before discussing their brain responses.

blocks.text: **Signed languages use a visual modality and manual and bodily articulators.** The hands, face and upper body contribute to a coordinated linguistic signal. Space can carry linguistic relations. Some signs are iconic, meaning that aspects of their form resemble aspects of their meaning.
children: Iconicity is easy to overestimate when a familiar translation is supplied. A visible resemblance does not eliminate the need to learn a language's forms and structure.

blocks.text: **Changing the articulators does not remove linguistic organization.** Signed languages remain structured systems rather than collections of transparent gestures.
children: The pictured signs include actions, objects and less directly depictable concepts. A gloss names the translation but does not make every feature of a sign self-explanatory.

blocks.text: **Fluent signing coordinates hands, facial expression, gaze and upper-body movement.** The linguistic signal is distributed across these visible articulators rather than produced by one hand movement at a time. Like speech, a fluent stream is continuous enough that word boundaries are not always obvious to a learner.
children: Eye contact and movement timing are therefore relevant to perceiving the interaction, alongside the form of individual signs.

blocks.text: **The unit of analysis is coordinated language production, not an isolated hand pose.** Fluency depends on how the articulators work together.
children: The linked demonstration invites attention to coordination and segmentation. The original video link is retained separately from the static slide.

blocks.text: **Signed-language phonology includes contrastive hand configuration, location and movement.** Changing one of these features can distinguish signs, just as changing a speech feature can distinguish spoken words. The PLEASE–SORRY and ONION–APPLE examples demonstrate that closely related visible forms can have different linguistic identities.
children: Phonology therefore concerns the organization of contrastive form, not only acoustic sound.

blocks.text: **A feature is linguistically contrastive when changing it changes the sign identity.** Visual similarity alone does not determine whether two forms belong to the same category.
children: The paired images hold some properties similar while contrasting others. Handshape, where the gesture is made and how it moves are separate dimensions to inspect.

blocks.text: **Categorical perception can be tested by varying a sign feature continuously.** The hand-configuration continuum moves between forms while the observer's identification and discrimination responses are measured. One continuum crosses a phonemic distinction between PLEASE and SORRY. The allophonic comparison varies hand configuration without the same change in sign identity.
children: A sharp identification boundary accompanied by better discrimination near that boundary would indicate category-sensitive perception.

blocks.text: **The test distinguishes a physical change from a linguistically meaningful category change.** Both continua vary visually, but only one crosses the relevant contrast.
children: The stimulus sequences progress through intermediate hand configurations. Comparing equal-sized changes within and across a linguistic boundary is more informative than comparing only the two endpoints.

blocks.text: **Deaf signers show a sharper categorical boundary for phonemic than allophonic hand-configuration changes.** In the phonemic condition, identification shifts steeply around stimuli 4–6. Discrimination is also strongest near the phonemic boundary. Comparable physical steps are easier to distinguish when they cross that category boundary.
children: The allophonic identification function is shallower and lacks the same localized discrimination peak. This links the perceptual pattern to linguistic contrast rather than any visible hand change.

blocks.text: **The combination of a sharp identification shift and a boundary-related discrimination peak supports categorical perception.** Identification alone would provide a less complete test.
children: The top plots show categorization and the lower plots discrimination. Compare the position of the steep change with the discrimination peak in the phonemic column.

blocks.text: **Signed languages can use positions in signing space to represent relationships.** A classifier sign made at a particular location can indicate the relative position of an object. Understanding a sentence can require retaining where entities were introduced and how subsequent signs relate to those locations.
children: Spatial processing therefore contributes to linguistic comprehension, rather than functioning only as background vision.

blocks.text: **Where a sign is made can be part of the sentence's meaning.** The listener must track linguistic relations across space as well as over time.
children: The classifier example uses relative placement to express a relation between objects. The signing location is instructional information, not a decorative feature of the display.

blocks.text: **Signed-language comprehension recruits classical language regions and shows left lateralization, as spoken-language comprehension does.** Inferior frontal and posterior superior temporal regions are part of this overlap. Signing also engages visual and superior parietal regions relevant to its perceptual and spatial demands.
children: The combination suggests both common language organization and modality-related contributions. Similarity does not require identical activation everywhere.

blocks.text: **Different sensory inputs can engage overlapping language networks.** The additional visual and spatial activity reflects the demands of processing a signed signal.
children: The figure compares deaf signers, hearing signers and hearing audiovisual-speech participants. Hearing signers are particularly useful because signing experience is not restricted to people who are deaf.

blocks.text: **Bavelier and colleagues compared hearing controls, deaf signers and hearing signers on visual attention.** Participants monitored dots for brief changes in luminance or velocity, with attention directed centrally or peripherally. Deaf participants showed an advantage when attention was directed to the periphery.
children: Including hearing signers helps separate experience with signing from lack of auditory input. If all signers had the same advantage, signing alone would be a stronger explanation.

blocks.text: **The comparison groups are essential to the causal question.** A deaf-versus-hearing contrast alone would bundle deafness and signing experience together.
children: The display distinguishes center and peripheral monitoring. Luminance concerns brightness and velocity concerns motion, so the task measures attention to brief visual changes rather than sign comprehension itself.

blocks.text: **Signing experience and deafness show different associations with visual processing.** Both deaf and hearing signers show a leftward shift in motion-processing lateralization relative to hearing nonsigners. Enhanced peripheral attention is found in deaf individuals, not hearing signers. Signing experience alone therefore does not explain that enhancement.
children: The proposed interpretations involve links between motion and language systems for signing, and reduced reliance on auditory peripheral cues in deafness.

blocks.text: **Do not combine lateralization and peripheral attention into one undifferentiated advantage.** They track different aspects of experience.
children: The upper comparison concerns hemispheric bias in motion-related areas. The lower comparison concerns center-versus-periphery attention. The sign and size of a bar must be read using its own axis.

blocks.text: **Comparing sign comprehension with another organized gesture system helps control visible movement demands.** Tic-tac uses sophisticated hand gestures to communicate horse-racing odds. Both tasks involve meaningful, sequenced hand movements. A difference between them is more informative about linguistic processing than a comparison between signing and no movement.
children: The control is not identical to a natural language, which is precisely why the remaining difference is of interest.

blocks.text: **A useful control shares some demands while differing in the process being tested.** Tic-tac helps separate language comprehension from hand-motion processing.
children: The original demonstration link concerns the control gesture system. The comparison does not assume that every meaningful gesture is a natural language.

blocks.text: **Sign language produces stronger activity around posterior superior temporal language regions than tic-tac gestures.** This supports a distinction between processing organized hand movements and processing a natural language. The comparison reduces a simple explanation based only on the presence of hands moving through space.
children: The frontal activation shown is superior to classic Broca's area, so it should not be casually relabeled as a precise Broca's effect.

blocks.text: **Shared visual movement does not explain the entire neural response to signed language.** The temporal-region difference is the central language-related result.
children: The highlighted posterior temporal activation is near Wernicke's region. The figure supports a regional comparison, not the claim that one highlighted spot is solely responsible for all signing.

blocks.text: **Signed languages have linguistic form, grammar and language-related neural organization.** Contrastive sign features can produce categorical perception, and comprehension recruits posterior superior temporal language regions. Signing experience is associated with changes in motion lateralization. Deafness is associated with enhanced peripheral attention in the reported comparison.
children: These findings jointly show that linguistic experience and sensory history contribute in different ways.

blocks.text: **A coherent account must separate shared language organization from sensory adaptations.** Neither “sign is just gesture” nor “modality makes no difference” captures the evidence.
children: The summary combines behavioral category evidence, group comparisons and neural contrasts. Each addresses a different question, so one result should not be used as if it established all the others.

blocks.text: **Comprehending a signed spatial description can require a perspective transformation.** A room can be described from the speaker's perspective or the addressee's perspective. The figure's caption reports better comprehension for descriptions from the speaker's perspective despite the mental transformation that this requires.
children: This illustrates that the most linguistically natural representation is not necessarily the one that eliminates every spatial transformation.

blocks.text: **Spatial comprehension depends on conventions as well as geometric convenience.** The observer may transform a speaker-centered description rather than prefer an already reversed one.
children: The two signing sequences describe the same table location in the room diagram. The difference is whose perspective organizes the description, not a change in the table's actual location.

blocks.text: **Braille represents written language through tactilely distinguishable symbols.** It is a way to read a language, rather than a separate natural language with its own grammar. The symbols are optimized for touch. Fingers acquire letters sequentially, creating perceptual demands that differ from viewing printed text.
children: The comparison asks how reading networks operate when the input arrives through touch instead of vision.

blocks.text: **The linguistic task can remain reading while the sensory input changes.** This makes Braille useful for studying cross-modal organization.
children: Sequential tactile sampling is a processing constraint. It does not imply that Braille readers must consciously name every individual dot before understanding a word.

blocks.text: **Braille reading activates visual cortex in blind individuals, with more extensive recruitment after earlier sight loss.** Early- and late-blind groups therefore provide a comparison of developmental sensory history. Early-blind participants show stronger involvement of regions associated with visual word processing than late-blind participants.
children: This indicates that a region's usual sensory label does not completely determine the information it can help process.

blocks.text: **The timing of sensory experience relates to later functional organization.** Visual cortex can participate in tactile reading even when the stimulus is not visual.
children: The early-blind examples are on the left and late-blind examples on the right. Compare the extent of activation rather than assuming that every displayed colored voxel has the same function.

blocks.text: **Merabet and colleagues tested rapid plasticity by blindfolding sighted adults for five days while training Braille.** A comparison group received training without the same continuous removal of visual input. The blindfolded group learned more quickly. This suggests that eliminating competing visual input can affect tactile learning over a short timescale.
children: Because the participants were sighted adults, the experiment tests a different question from lifelong or early blindness.

blocks.text: **Cross-modal changes do not have to be limited to early development.** A short-term manipulation can reveal latent contributions to tactile processing.
children: The procedure includes baseline testing, training, repeated imaging and blindfold removal. The group comparison distinguishes training effects from the additional effect of continuous blindfolding.

blocks.text: **Visual-cortex responses to Braille developed during blindfolding and reversed after the blindfold was removed on Day 6.** The time course shows that the change was rapid and reversible. Removing visual input can allow tactile-related activity to become more evident. Restoring vision changes that balance again.
children: This pattern is consistent with unmasking existing inputs rather than requiring the creation of an entirely new pathway over a few days.

blocks.text: **Reversibility helps constrain the mechanism.** A rapid response that disappears after vision returns suggests a change in functional contribution or competition.
children: The images and signal plot compare Days 1, 3, 5 and 6. Day 6 is specifically the post-blindfold condition, not simply another day under unchanged deprivation.

blocks.text: **Disrupting visual cortex with TMS impaired Braille discrimination in the blindfolded group.** This goes beyond showing that the region becomes active during touch. On Day 5, the blindfolded group's error rate rises under 1 Hz TMS relative to its baseline and sham conditions. The nonblindfolded group does not show the same selective disruption.
children: The effect is no longer present in the same way after blindfold removal. The result supports a temporary functional contribution of visual cortex to tactile performance.

blocks.text: **Activation and necessity are different kinds of evidence.** Interfering with a region and changing behavior provides stronger evidence that its activity contributes to the task.
children: The solid symbols identify blindfolded participants. The vertical axis is error rate, so the upward TMS change means worse performance, not improved reading.

blocks.text: **Language-related organization is resilient across sensory modalities while remaining shaped by experience.** Signed language recruits classical language regions, and Braille engages networks associated with text processing. Competition among available inputs offers a way to understand reorganization. When an input is absent or reduced, other information can make a larger contribution.
children: The evidence does not imply that all regions are interchangeable. It shows both stable functional relationships and experience-sensitive recruitment.

blocks.text: **A brain region's contribution reflects development and competition as well as its usual sensory input.** Common language functions can coexist with modality-specific adaptations.
children: Distinguish the language-network overlap from the visual-attention and tactile-recruitment findings. They support a related account of plasticity through different experimental comparisons.

blocks.text: **Orthographic depth** describes how consistently spelling corresponds to pronunciation. English is relatively deep because many spellings do not transparently specify their sounds. COLONEL and PARADIGM make the problem concrete. Applying common letter–sound patterns can produce a plausible-looking pronunciation that is wrong for the actual word.
children: In shallower writing systems, such as Finnish and Korean, spelling–sound correspondences are more predictable. The comparison concerns the writing system, not the intelligence or ability of its readers.

blocks.text: **An unfamiliar spelling cannot always be decoded correctly from its letters alone.** Deep orthographies create more exceptions that readers must learn through experience.
children: The English examples contrast ordinary expectations from the letters with the word's learned pronunciation. A deep script is less predictable, not completely random.

blocks.text: **Finnish has a shallow orthography.** Letters correspond relatively unambiguously to phonemes, so learning a spelling–sound correspondence helps with many different words. Doubled letters represent a meaningful length distinction. A doubled consonant is geminated, and a doubled vowel is long.
children: This regularity helps Finnish children learn decoding quickly. Decoding means generating a pronunciation from a written form, whether or not its meaning is familiar.

blocks.text: **Consistent correspondences make decoding easier to generalize.** Finnish readers can apply what they learn about letters to unfamiliar written forms.
children: The linked Finnish lesson is a source demonstration. Its sound is not embedded in the PDF, so the written claims establish the correspondence and length distinctions without supplying a recovered recording.

blocks.text: **Pseudoword reading tests decoding.** Because a pseudoword is not a familiar stored word, the child must generalize from learned spelling–sound patterns. The comparison involves Grade 1 children learning different alphabetic writing systems. Children learning many other languages produce plausible pseudoword pronunciations more successfully than English learners.
children: English's less predictable correspondences help explain why decoding develops more slowly. This task does not measure the child's entire language ability.

blocks.text: **A made-up word separates decoding from remembering a familiar word.** The lower English performance is consistent with greater orthographic depth.
children: Compare accuracy across languages for the same type of task. The important outcome is the relative difficulty of English pseudoword decoding, not a claim that English children cannot decode.

blocks.text: **Korean writing represents sound structure systematically.** Related phonemes can have related written shapes, so the visual forms themselves reflect aspects of phonological organization. The letters are arranged into syllable blocks with initial, medial and sometimes final positions. Those positions are not three unrelated pictures of whole words.
children: The velar consonant forms share the basic angular ㄱ shape. Additional strokes or doubling distinguish related consonants.

blocks.text: **The organization of Hangul supports more than consistent pronunciation.** Similar sound categories can also be visibly related in their written symbols.
children: The diagrams label initial, medial and final positions. The g, kk and k examples share a shape family, illustrating how a place-of-articulation relation can be reflected in the script.

blocks.text: **Frequency and regularity interact.** Low-frequency exception words are slowed much more than low-frequency regular words, whereas high-frequency words show a much smaller regularity difference. Naming latency is the time needed to begin saying the word. Higher values mean slower responses.
children: An interaction means the effect of one factor depends on the other. The regularity cost is not a fixed amount added equally to high- and low-frequency words.

blocks.text: **Experience matters especially when pronunciation conflicts with the usual spelling pattern.** Frequent exposure reduces the disadvantage of exception words.
children: The lines are close at high frequency and separate at low frequency. Exception words rise to roughly 580 ms, while regular words rise only to roughly 555 ms in this figure.

blocks.text: **A dual-route interpretation separates lexical retrieval from sublexical decoding.** The lexical process supplies the learned pronunciation of a particular word, while decoding computes pronunciation from spelling units. For a high-frequency word, lexical information becomes available quickly enough to reduce the influence of the decoding output.
children: For a low-frequency exception, the lexical response is less efficient and the regularized decoding output can interfere. Nonwords depend on decoding because they lack a stored whole-word entry.

blocks.text: **Two routes can explain why regularity matters most for unfamiliar words.** Fast lexical processing protects familiar exceptions from competing sublexical output.
children: This is an interpretation of the interaction, not the interaction itself. Other architectures must be evaluated against the same observed pattern.

blocks.text: **In a PDP account, rules are generalizations learned across words.** Whole-word knowledge is distributed across learned mappings instead of being stored only in a distinct lexical route. The same learning mechanism can capture both patterns shared by many words and information specific to a familiar word.
children: The research strategy asks whether domain-general learning can explain reading. This contrasts with choosing separate adult processing components primarily from neuropsychological dissociations.

blocks.text: **Word-specific knowledge and generalization can coexist in the same learned system.** They do not have to be implemented as a dictionary and a separate symbolic rule list.
children: “Distributed” refers to how knowledge is represented across the network. It does not mean that the model has no memory of individual words.

blocks.text: **A learned network can produce a frequency-by-regularity interaction without separate frequency and rule mechanisms.** Regular words receive support from patterns shared across many words. An exception conflicts with those patterns, so learning its particular mapping is especially important. Frequent exposure strengthens that word-specific mapping.
children: A low-frequency exception has both weak item-specific learning and poor support from the dominant pattern. This combination creates a larger disadvantage than either factor alone.

blocks.text: **Consistency supplies support from other words, while frequency strengthens experience with the particular word.** Their joint influence explains why infrequent exceptions are especially difficult.
children: The interaction is shared evidence that both architectures must explain. Producing it does not by itself establish whether the implementation contains symbolic rules.

blocks.text: **A PDP model can pronounce nonwords using the weights learned from real words.** A new spelling activates patterns that overlap with familiar spellings, allowing the network to generalize. No stored entry for the particular nonword is required. The same learned correspondences that support consistent words can support a new combination.
children: This is a proposed mechanism for decoding without a separate GPC rule module.

blocks.text: **Novel pronunciation can result from applying learned statistical structure.** Nonword reading therefore does not automatically establish a separate symbolic route.
children: The relevant comparison is whether one learned mapping can handle both familiar words and new items. The claim must still be checked against the model's actual performance.

blocks.text: **Poor nonword performance can challenge either a theoretical proposal or a particular implementation.** The early model's nonword accuracy was weaker than desired. One possibility is that a single associative mechanism cannot explain the task. Another is that the chosen representations fail to capture the similarities needed for generalization.
children: Improving the implementation while retaining the theoretical mechanism helps distinguish these possibilities.

blocks.text: **A failed simulation does not identify its own cause.** The failure must be traced to the architecture, learning assumptions, representations or other implementation choices.
children: The important question is what changes when the model is repaired. A representational improvement is a different theoretical move from adding a separate nonword route.

blocks.text: **Generalization depends on how sound similarity is represented.** The early Seidenberg–McClelland model used Wickelfeatures, whose representation of phonology was problematic for nonword reading. Plaut and colleagues improved the phonological representations and obtained better nonword performance. This supports a representational explanation for at least part of the earlier failure.
children: Behavioral relations between phonological processing and decoding also make phonology a relevant target for explanation.

blocks.text: **Changing the representation can improve decoding without adding a symbolic rule system.** That distinction matters when evaluating the original theoretical claim.
children: The comparison concerns models with different representations. Better performance after that change is evidence about implementation, not proof that every associative model will succeed.

blocks.text: **A network generalizes through similarity.** If its phonological representation poorly captures similarities among words, the learned mapping cannot transfer as effectively to new forms. A familiar word can retain support from its own training history. A nonword lacks that item-specific experience and depends more heavily on generalization.
children: This produces a reason for unfamiliar forms to be especially vulnerable to poor representations without requiring a dedicated nonword mechanism.

blocks.text: **The same representational weakness can have unequal effects on words and nonwords.** Familiarity can partly compensate where new-item generalization cannot.
children: Distinguish a weaker shared representation from damage to a separate route. Both can create a task difference, but they locate the explanation differently.

blocks.text: **Harm and Seidenberg manipulated noise in phonological representations.** Increasing noise makes the sound representations less reliable while keeping the model's general learning framework. The manipulation produced poorer nonword decoding and relative sparing of word recognition. It also linked the severity of the phonological deficit to the degree of decoding difficulty.
children: The model therefore connects a reading pattern to the quality of a more general phonological system.

blocks.text: **A selective-looking reading deficit can emerge from degraded shared representations.** Nonwords are especially dependent on reliable generalization.
children: Noise is the manipulated model property. Word and nonword performance are outcomes, so the simulation tests a directional mechanistic proposal rather than merely observing a correlation.

blocks.text: **The lexicon and grammar offer different ways to produce a past tense.** Lexical retrieval supplies an irregular form such as HELD, while grammatical combination can produce WALK plus -ed. Pinker and Ullman's diagram associates lexical lookup with declarative memory and grammatical combination with procedural processing.
children: Like dual-route reading, the account separates word-specific knowledge from a productive operation. Unlike reading aloud, its task is to transform a stem according to a grammatical feature, rather than convert spelling into sound.

blocks.text: **Similar-looking architectures can solve different computational problems.** Keep morphological inflection separate from grapheme–phoneme conversion.
children: The input includes a stem and a past-tense feature. The diagram distinguishes lexical association from combination, and its blocking connection prevents a retrieved irregular from competing unchecked with a regular form.

blocks.text: **The Words and Rules proposal was motivated partly by a theory of grammar.** A categorical symbolic grammar describes productive patterns, but language also contains exceptions. Reading dual-route theories were strongly motivated by neuropsychological dissociations. The morphology proposal also reflects a commitment to keeping the grammatical rule system distinct from exceptional lexical information.
**The motivation for an architecture matters when evaluating its evidence.** Similar diagrams do not mean that the theories were derived from the same observations.
children: The contrast is between a dissociation-driven reading account and a grammatical argument for separating productive rules from exceptions.

blocks.text: **An associative lexicon handles information that does not fit a categorical rule.** Its representations are word-specific and sensitive to frequency and phonological similarity. KEEP–KEPT, WEEP–WEPT and LEAP–LEAPT illustrate similarity among irregular forms. An exception can belong to a small family rather than being wholly unrelated to other words.
children: Assigning these properties to lexical memory lets the rule system remain categorical and general.

blocks.text: **Separating exceptions protects a simple rule, but creates a second mechanism that must also be explained.** The associative system carries graded and item-specific influences.
children: The shared sound pattern in the listed verbs motivates associative similarity. It is not evidence that every irregular verb uses exactly the same transformation.

blocks.text: **Rumelhart and McClelland modeled past tense as a learned association between present and past sound patterns.** A single trainable network learns across verbs instead of applying a separately specified -ed rule. The model encodes a root's phonology, transforms that representation through modifiable connections, and decodes an output pattern.
children: Regularity is a pattern learned from many examples. Irregular forms are also learned within the same system.

blocks.text: **One learning mechanism is proposed for both regularities and exceptions.** The challenge is to explain accurate generalization as well as familiar forms.
children: The fixed encoding and decoding stages surround a modifiable pattern associator. Wickelfeatures represent sound patterns, while the trainable connections store the learned mapping.

blocks.text: **U-shaped learning describes an initial success, a decline, and later recovery.** A child may correctly say RAN, later produce RUNNED, and eventually return to RAN. The middle error is a **regularization**, because the child applies the common past-tense pattern to an irregular verb.
children: The decline does not necessarily mean that the child has stopped learning. A changing system can generalize more broadly while temporarily disrupting an earlier correct response.

blocks.text: **Development can involve temporary errors as knowledge changes.** A theory must explain the entire trajectory, not just the final adult response.
children: The vertical dimension is successful performance and the horizontal dimension is development or training. A U shape concerns accuracy over time, not the shape of a word.

blocks.text: **The Words and Rules account explains U-shaped learning through changes in the use of rules and lexical exceptions.** Early correct forms can be imitated before a productive rule is available. When the rule is learned, it can be applied too broadly, yielding RUNNED. Later, learned irregulars and the blocking process prevent that regularization.
children: This account treats the developmental stages as involving distinguishable processes rather than only gradual changes in one mapping.

blocks.text: **Overregularization is interpreted as productive rule use that is not yet sufficiently constrained by exceptions.** Recovery depends on the irregular form winning over the rule output.
children: Blocking means that retrieval of the appropriate irregular prevents the otherwise available regular form. It is a proposed mechanism, not merely another name for correct performance.

blocks.text: **Changing the training vocabulary can produce U-shaped learning in one network.** Early training emphasizes frequent irregular verbs, allowing those particular mappings to be learned. As more regular verbs enter training, their common pattern changes the network's responses. That generalization can interfere with previously learned irregulars.
children: With further learning, the network can recover the irregular responses while retaining broad regularity. No new symbolic rule component is inserted at the point of decline.

blocks.text: **A shift in the distribution of experience can temporarily disrupt familiar responses.** The learning account explains the developmental pattern through changing weights and input.
children: The lower plot contrasts correct irregular responses with regularized alternatives. Their changing strengths illustrate competition during training, rather than the sudden appearance of a separate rule box.

blocks.text: **Testing untrained verbs asks whether the network learned transferable structure.** A real English verb can be novel to a model if it was excluded from that model's training set. The test therefore uses the logic of a wug task even when the items are real words to humans.
children: The model can generate many appropriate past-tense features, but feature-level success must be distinguished from producing an entirely correct word.

blocks.text: **Generalization is defined relative to the learner's experience.** A familiar human word is still a valid novel-model test when it was withheld from training.
children: The summary reports proportions of Wickelfeatures generated correctly. A high proportion of correct features does not imply that the same proportion of whole words was pronounced perfectly.

blocks.text: **Some model outputs contain changes that are unlike ordinary human regularizations.** Examples include MADE(D)-like changes to MATE and the unusual outputs MEMBLED for MAIL and TOUREDER for TOUR. The model authors acknowledge that people are unlikely to make some of these errors. They suggest that additional output constraints could reduce bizarre responses.
children: This separates capturing an overall learning pattern from matching the detailed form of human errors.

blocks.text: **A plausible learning curve is not enough if the model produces implausible words.** Error structure provides another test of the representation and decoding process.
children: The quotation discusses outputs near threshold and a possible cleanup mechanism. That proposed mechanism is an explanation to be tested, not a repair already demonstrated by the quoted result.

blocks.text: **Joanisse and Seidenberg propose that phonology supports rule-like generalization while semantics especially supports irregular forms.** The same system links speech input, meaning and speech output. Reliable sound representations support extension from familiar present–past pairs to new forms. Irregular mappings receive additional support from the particular word's semantic representation.
children: The hypothesis concerns different degrees of dependence on shared systems, rather than a separate symbolic rule route for every regular response.

blocks.text: **The regular–irregular contrast can arise from how phonological and semantic information contribute.** A graded system can produce systematic differences between item types.
children: The diagram connects speech input and semantics through learned mappings to speech output. Its components represent domains of information, not a list of regular and irregular words in separate boxes.

blocks.text: **The model aims to explain the dissociation between irregular and nonword past-tense performance.** These tasks differ in how much they depend on learned word-specific information and phonological generalization. A nonword has no familiar item-specific semantic history to support its inflection. A known irregular can require semantic support because its output is not well predicted by the dominant pattern.
children: Manipulating phonological or semantic integrity tests whether these different dependencies can produce opposite impairment profiles.

blocks.text: **The same architecture should explain both sides of the patient pattern.** Selectivity must arise from the manipulated representations and their contribution to the task.
children: The target is a pattern of performance across item types. Drawing phonology and semantics in a diagram is not enough unless damaging them produces the relevant outcomes.

blocks.text: **The patient pattern associated here with Broca's aphasia includes especially poor nonword past-tense production.** These patients have left anterior injury and difficulty producing speech. Regular forms are also vulnerable, while irregular forms are relatively better in the displayed comparison. A novel BLICK must be transformed without relying on a familiar stored past tense.
children: This motivates investigating phonological contributions to the apparent morphological deficit.

blocks.text: **Difficulty with productive inflection may be connected to sound processing.** The nonword condition is particularly demanding because it relies on generalization.
children: The graph places nonword accuracy below regular and irregular accuracy. The irregular advantage over regulars is smaller than the nonword disadvantage, so these differences should not be treated as equally large.

blocks.text: **Other patient groups show a larger problem with irregular past-tense forms.** The material discusses Wernicke's and Alzheimer's patients and anomic patients with inferior or middle temporal injury. Their irregular performance is lower than their regular and nonword performance in the displayed comparison.
children: This creates the other side of the dissociation and motivates examining the information that especially supports known irregular forms.

blocks.text: **Relatively preserved nonword inflection can coexist with poor irregular inflection.** The theory must explain this reverse pattern as well as phonological impairment.
children: The middle bar is the irregular condition, at roughly 60% correct, compared with higher regular and nonword scores. The diagnostic labels do not make every individual's performance identical.

blocks.text: **The classical contrast associates Wernicke's aphasia with fluent but often poorly interpretable speech and Broca's aphasia with effortful, telegraphic speech.** The former can include neologisms, while the latter can omit grammatical particles and show word-order difficulty. This makes a lexical-versus-grammatical interpretation attractive. However, a descriptive syndrome is not itself a demonstration of an isolated processing module.
children: Content words may be relatively preserved in telegraphic speech, while fluent speech can retain sentence-like structure without conveying a clear message.

blocks.text: **Fluency, grammatical organization and meaningful word selection are distinguishable dimensions.** The two example profiles emphasize different disruptions.
children: The quoted utterances contrast fluent but difficult-to-interpret output with short, effortful content-word sequences. The diagnostic terms summarize patterns rather than guaranteeing identical symptoms in every patient.

blocks.text: **Broca's original patients are not necessarily straightforward examples of what is now called Broca's aphasia.** Profound inability to articulate speech can reflect motor-planning impairment rather than a selective grammatical deficit. **Apraxia of speech** concerns planning or coordinating speech movements. That differs from explaining an omission of grammatical structure in otherwise producible speech.
children: The historical label therefore should not substitute for a precise description of the impaired behavior.

blocks.text: **A familiar syndrome name does not settle which level of processing is affected.** Articulation and grammatical formulation must be distinguished.
children: The case description emphasizes extremely restricted spoken output despite some preserved understanding. It motivates examining speech production at multiple levels rather than locating grammar from the name alone.

blocks.text: **A grammar–lexicon distinction makes the classical aphasia contrast theoretically appealing.** A grammatical system combines forms, while lexical knowledge concerns words and their properties. Chomsky's example of a grammatical but semantically unusual sentence shows that syntactic well-formedness cannot be reduced to whether a sentence describes a sensible event.
children: That conceptual distinction does not establish a simple one-to-one mapping from each syndrome to one isolated component.

blocks.text: **Syntax and meaning can come apart in a judgment without proving a perfectly modular neural organization.** The behavioral and theoretical claims should be kept separate.
children: “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” contrasts with an order that violates English syntax. The example isolates grammatical organization from familiarity or ordinary plausibility.

blocks.text: **The functional level selects word meanings and semantic roles, while the positional level organizes word forms into a grammatical sequence.** Phonological encoding and articulation concern later aspects of producing the utterance. A **lemma** is a representation involved in lexical selection, distinct from simply executing its sound pattern. Positional processing contributes ordering and morphological structure.
children: Combinations such as HOUSEBOAT show that complex-word meaning can be partly compositional. Errors such as “easy enoughly” provide evidence about the organization of morphological operations.

blocks.text: **Word selection, ordering, sound encoding and articulation are different explanatory levels.** An apparent lexical–grammatical contrast should be related to those operations carefully.
children: The diagram runs from message-level conceptual preparation through functional and positional levels to phonological encoding and speech gestures. Its order represents a processing proposal, not a direct picture of separate brain locations.

blocks.text: **Egocentric spatial descriptions use the speaker's position and orientation.** Left, right, in front and behind are familiar examples for nearby objects. Tzeltal commonly uses absolute directions in circumstances where English speakers might use these relative terms.
children: The contrast motivates asking whether habitual language use relates to nonverbal spatial coding, rather than merely comparing two ways of giving spoken directions.

blocks.text: **A direction can stay fixed when a person turns.** Absolute coding differs from coding an object as being on the viewer's left.
children: The language comparison concerns preferred spatial descriptions. It does not imply that speakers of either language are incapable of learning another frame.

blocks.text: **Tzeltal's uphill and downhill terms function as an absolute directional system.** Their historical connection to a slope does not mean that each use simply points to the nearest visible hill. A direction is retained as a stable spatial reference rather than being recalculated from the speaker's current left and right.
children: This allows positions to be described consistently as the speaker changes orientation.

blocks.text: **A landmark origin and an absolute use are different properties.** A historically landscape-based term can become a stable directional reference.
children: The contrast is with a description that depends entirely on the current viewpoint. The relevant feature is how the reference behaves across changes in location and orientation.

blocks.text: **The chips task separates relative from absolute spatial memory by rotating the participant 180 degrees.** A participant sees a configuration, waits, and then chooses its match at a second table. A relative response preserves the arrangement with respect to the person's viewpoint. An absolute response preserves its orientation in the environment, so the two responses diverge after rotation.
children: Dutch speakers predominantly gave relative responses, while Tzeltal speakers gave more absolute responses. The association is consistent with their preferred linguistic frames but does not isolate language from all other experience.

blocks.text: **The rotation makes two otherwise similar descriptions predict different choices.** The nonverbal response reveals a preferred spatial coding strategy.
children: The north arrow stays fixed while the person changes orientation. Red bars represent relative choices and blue bars absolute choices, showing different response distributions across the two language groups.

blocks.text: **Spatial inference can combine relations learned in different displays.** Participants learn the relation between two objects, rotate to another display, and learn a second relation involving a shared object. They then place an object relative to another using the combined information. Relative and absolute coding lead to different placements because the person's orientation has changed.
children: Dutch and Tzeltal response patterns again differ in the direction associated with their preferred spatial frames.

blocks.text: **The task goes beyond reproducing one remembered arrangement.** It asks whether a frame is used when combining spatial relations to make an inference.
children: The cube appears in both learning displays, linking the cone and cylinder relations. The final placement distinguishes a viewer-relative inference from one preserving environmental direction.

blocks.text: **Testing conditions could contribute to the apparent language-group difference.** Li and Gleitman noted that Tzeltal participants had been tested with visible, familiar outdoor landmarks, unlike many laboratory participants. An environment with useful landmarks can encourage landmark-based coding. A windowless laboratory can make viewer-relative descriptions more convenient.
children: Manipulating landmark availability within English speakers tests whether the behavior can change without changing native language.

blocks.text: **A language comparison can be confounded with a setting comparison.** The environment must be considered before assigning the entire difference to linguistic structure.
children: The critical contrast is access to spatial cues, not simply the label “laboratory.” Windows, outdoor views and familiar surroundings can alter which references are useful.

blocks.text: **English speakers' preference for relative coding weakened when external landmarks were available.** They strongly preferred relative responses with the blinds down, but the preference was less pronounced with a street view or outdoors. The manipulation changes the spatial information available while keeping the language group the same.
children: This demonstrates that task context can influence the response. It challenges an explanation in which language alone fixes the chosen frame.

blocks.text: **Spatial strategy is sensitive to the testing environment.** A within-language change helps reveal a potential confound in a between-language comparison.
children: A reduced relative preference is not necessarily a complete switch to absolute coding. Describe the observed change in preference without exaggerating it into an all-or-none reversal.

blocks.text: **Levinson and colleagues argued that the simplified task could make the experimenter's purpose too obvious.** Low memory demands and short time or distance between displays may encourage a deliberate strategy about rotation. Participants who infer what is being tested can alter their response for reasons different from habitual spatial coding.
children: The response therefore focuses on memory load and task transparency, rather than denying that landmarks can ever matter.

blocks.text: **Changing a task can change the process it measures.** A landmark effect in an easy, transparent task may not settle how people habitually remember spatial relations.
children: The proposed alternative is a demand-characteristic explanation. Participants' interpretation of the experiment may influence the response independently of their normal coding preference.

blocks.text: **Categorical perception can be tested by varying a sign feature continuously.** The hand-configuration continuum moves between forms while the observer's identification and discrimination responses are measured. One continuum crosses a phonemic distinction between PLEASE and SORRY. The allophonic comparison varies hand configuration without the same change in sign identity.
children: A sharp identification boundary accompanied by better discrimination near that boundary would indicate category-sensitive perception.

blocks.text: **The test distinguishes a physical change from a linguistically meaningful category change.** Both continua vary visually, but only one crosses the relevant contrast.
children: The stimulus sequences progress through intermediate hand configurations. Comparing equal-sized changes within and across a linguistic boundary is more informative than comparing only the two endpoints.

blocks.text: **Deaf signers show a sharper categorical boundary for phonemic than allophonic hand-configuration changes.** In the phonemic condition, identification shifts steeply around stimuli 4–6. Discrimination is also strongest near the phonemic boundary. Comparable physical steps are easier to distinguish when they cross that category boundary.
children: The allophonic identification function is shallower and lacks the same localized discrimination peak. This links the perceptual pattern to linguistic contrast rather than any visible hand change.

blocks.text: **The combination of a sharp identification shift and a boundary-related discrimination peak supports categorical perception.** Identification alone would provide a less complete test.
children: The top plots show categorization and the lower plots discrimination. Compare the position of the steep change with the discrimination peak in the phonemic column.

blocks.text: **Signed-language comprehension recruits classical language regions and shows left lateralization, as spoken-language comprehension does.** Inferior frontal and posterior superior temporal regions are part of this overlap. Signing also engages visual and superior parietal regions relevant to its perceptual and spatial demands.
children: The combination suggests both common language organization and modality-related contributions. Similarity does not require identical activation everywhere.

blocks.text: **Different sensory inputs can engage overlapping language networks.** The additional visual and spatial activity reflects the demands of processing a signed signal.
children: The figure compares deaf signers, hearing signers and hearing audiovisual-speech participants. Hearing signers are particularly useful because signing experience is not restricted to people who are deaf.

blocks.text: **Signed languages have linguistic form, grammar and language-related neural organization.** Contrastive sign features can produce categorical perception, and comprehension recruits posterior superior temporal language regions. Signing experience is associated with changes in motion lateralization. Deafness is associated with enhanced peripheral attention in the reported comparison.
children: These findings jointly show that linguistic experience and sensory history contribute in different ways.

blocks.text: **A coherent account must separate shared language organization from sensory adaptations.** Neither “sign is just gesture” nor “modality makes no difference” captures the evidence.
children: The summary combines behavioral category evidence, group comparisons and neural contrasts. Each addresses a different question, so one result should not be used as if it established all the others.

blocks.text: **The exercise hypothesis proposes that early language use preserves language-learning capacity, while the maturational-state hypothesis allows capacity to decline despite early use.** Both assume an early advantage, but they differ in what early successful experience protects. Later second-language difficulty in people who already acquired a first language is more directly compatible with maturation than with complete preservation through exercise.
children: This does not make early first-language experience unimportant. Early access and age-related change address related but distinct questions.

blocks.text: **A late L2 learner has already exercised language capacity.** That history is what makes late-L2 outcomes informative for distinguishing the two proposals.
children: The two text panels differ in the condition attached to decline. The exercise account includes preservation through use, while the maturational-state account predicts decline with maturation itself.

blocks.text: **Mayberry, Lock and Kazmi compared later language learning after different early-language histories.** Deaf individuals without accessible early language performed worse than those who had acquired an early spoken or signed language. Children first exposed to ASL at ages 9–15 had particular difficulty when it was also their first language. Those who had first learned a spoken language did much better, and the differences persisted.
children: The comparison distinguishes late first-language learning from late acquisition of an additional language.

blocks.text: **Age of starting ASL is not the same as age of first language access.** Earlier linguistic experience can support learning a new language later.
children: The bars separate no-early-language groups from early spoken or signed language groups. The contrast concerns access to language, not a simple superiority of speech over signing.

blocks.text: **Semantic blocking effects must be separated from visual-recognition difficulty.** Objects from one semantic category could resemble one another visually, creating a potential confound in naming. The materials were normed so that same-category items were not more visually similar on average. A separate visual-similarity manipulation also produced a different time course.
children: Visual blocking affected the first block, whereas the semantic pattern of interest developed differently. This weakens a purely visual explanation.

blocks.text: **A control is informative when it tests the alternative mechanism directly.** Matching appearance and manipulating visual similarity provide complementary evidence.
children: The comparison concerns when interference appears across repetitions. A difference in time course helps distinguish visual recognition from the proposed lexical contribution.

blocks.text: **Belke and colleagues presented four objects simultaneously but required their names in sequence.** This tests whether the absence of an effect in another simultaneous-display study depended on presentation format. Displaying all objects at once reduces dependence on a succession of isolated pictures. Serial naming still requires selecting and producing one label after another.
children: Eye tracking provides additional timing information about the processing of each object.

blocks.text: **Separating display timing from naming order helps locate the source of interference.** Simultaneous visibility does not remove the need for sequential lexical selection.
children: The four pictured animals are visible together. The instruction concerns producing their names in order, rather than choosing only one target from the display.

blocks.text: **Eye movements and speech onsets provide different timing measures during serial naming.** Gaze duration records how long the eyes remain on an object, while eye–speech lag concerns the interval between leaving it and beginning its spoken name. A participant can move the eyes toward the next object before articulating the current one. The measures therefore separate overlapping parts of preparation.
children: Different blocking effects on these measures can help constrain the processing stage affected.

blocks.text: **One total naming time can conceal several processes.** Coordinating eye and speech measures reveals where a condition begins to change performance.
children: The GD boxes represent gaze durations and the lag boxes extend toward articulatory onset. The timeline shows why looking at an object and speaking its name are not the same event.

blocks.text: **Semantic blocking increases gaze duration after the first presentation cycle, but not overall speech duration or eye–speech lag.** The measures therefore do not show a uniform slowdown. Speech duration decreases with repetition without a blocking difference. Gaze duration shows the condition difference after the first cycle.
children: The nonsignificant lag difference should not be reported as evidence for a reversed effect. The reported pattern is interpreted as supporting a contribution at lemma selection rather than articulation or phonological encoding.

blocks.text: **The location of the effect across measures matters more than a general statement that naming is slower.** Its time course and selectivity constrain the proposed mechanism.
children: HOM and HET compare homogeneous and heterogeneous contexts. The three panels correspond to speech duration, gaze duration and lag, so their vertical scales describe different measurements.

blocks.text: **McMurray and colleagues tested whether fine phonetic information affects lexical competition.** Participants heard a /b/–/p/ continuum while viewing pictures including BEAR and PEAR, with eye movements recorded. **Voice onset time**, or VOT, varies the timing between release and voicing. It can change how strongly the sound supports /b/ or /p/.
children: A thresholded account would pass a completed categorical decision onward. A cascaded account allows graded information to influence word candidates before uncertainty is fully resolved.

blocks.text: **The critical test is whether within-category differences influence lexical responses.** A binary final choice alone may hide that information.
children: The visual-world display includes a target, a phonetic competitor and unrelated fillers. Looking at the competitor is informative because its name overlaps with the heard word near the manipulated contrast.

blocks.text: **Participants selected the picture that best matched the spoken item.** Their BEAR–PEAR choices produced a typical step-like identification function across VOT. Shorter VOTs favored the /b/ response and longer VOTs the /p/ response. Near the boundary, the preferred category changed rapidly.
children: A categorical-looking final response does not establish that all earlier lexical activation was categorical.

blocks.text: **A forced choice can end in one category even when processing used graded evidence.** Eye movements provide a separate measure of that processing.
children: The horizontal axis is VOT in milliseconds and the vertical axis is proportion of /p/ responses. The steep transition is around 17.5 ms in the displayed function.

blocks.text: **Competitor looks vary with phonetic ambiguity even within a chosen category.** Tokens closer to the /b/–/p/ boundary produce more competition than clear tokens farther from it. A participant can ultimately select BEAR while spending more time looking at PEAR when the sound is close to the boundary.
children: This supports the claim that fine phonetic information remains relevant to lexical activation, rather than disappearing completely after a categorical phoneme decision.

blocks.text: **Final identification and moment-by-moment competition reveal different aspects of processing.** A sharp choice boundary can coexist with graded lexical uncertainty.
children: The gaze curves group trials by VOT and final response. The effect concerns looks to the unchosen competitor, not merely how often participants click the wrong picture.

blocks.text: **Competitor fixation increases as a token approaches the category boundary from either side.** For BEAR responses, more /p/-like VOT increases looks to PEAR. For PEAR responses, more /b/-like VOT increases looks to BEAR. The graph separates early and late observation windows. The gradient remains visible in the later competition measure, supporting continued sensitivity to within-category phonetic detail.
children: The result favors cascaded use of graded evidence over a model that transmits only a completed phoneme label with all within-category detail discarded.

blocks.text: **The relevant predictor is distance from the boundary, not only which side of it the token occupies.** Similar final choices can still have different lexical-competition profiles.
children: The left and right halves plot different final-response categories and their corresponding competitors. Early is 300–1100 ms and late is 1100–1900 ms, so the line types distinguish time windows rather than two participant groups.
